questions.q: How much electricity does it take to make a song with AI (like Suno or Udio)?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Radio and press pieces ask why AI music is bad for the environment (Q107 'Ongoing History Daily', https://q107.com/news/11676408/ongoing-history-daily-why-ai-generated-music-is-bad-for-the-environment/); The Baffler notes Suno's details aren't public (https://thebaffler.com/latest/its-not-easy-being-green-arcand).
questions.verdict: For the open music models that have been measured, it ranges from about one image's worth of energy to a few images' worth per 30-second clip. Suno and Udio publish nothing.
questions.answer: A September 2026 benchmark measured three open text-to-music models making 30-second clips on a single server GPU. GPU energy per generation was 0.2 Wh for ACE-Step, 1.7 Wh for MusicGen Large and 7.7 Wh for Stable Audio Open. That is roughly 0.2 to 6 times one AI image at 1.22 Wh. These numbers cover the GPU board only, not the CPU, cooling or the rest of the data centre, so the real total is higher. Full-length songs with vocals from commercial services like Suno or Udio have never been measured publicly, so their energy is unknown.

figures.claim: GPU energy per 30-second music generation: ACE-Step v1 3.5B 0.2 Wh, MusicGen Large 1.7 Wh, Stable Audio Open 1.0 7.7 Wh (Table 2a)
figures.quote: Latency is reported as mean ± SD in seconds, RAM/VRAM in GB, GPU utilization in %, GPU energy in Wh, and Cost in USD.
figures.publisher: Adorni, Papandrea, Rimoldi, Leidi (SUPSI / t2b AG), TTM-Bench, arXiv Sep 2026

questions.q: How much electricity did the viral Ghibli-style AI image trend use?
questions.evidence_people_ask: After Sam Altman said OpenAI's 'GPUs are melting' (TechRadar, https://www.techradar.com/computing/artificial-intelligence/our-gpus-are-melting-openai-puts-limits-on-image-creation-and-delays-rollout-to-free-accounts), commentators asked about the real cost (Shelly Palmer, https://shellypalmer.com/2025/03/our-gpus-are-melting-the-real-cost-of-ai-image-generation/).
questions.verdict: Nobody published the real figure. A rough estimate is hundreds to a couple of thousand megawatt-hours: a tiny slice of world data-centre use, though large for one feature in one week.
questions.answer: OpenAI said users made over 700 million images in the first week after ChatGPT's new image tool launched in March 2025. OpenAI has never said how much energy one of those images takes, and its model works differently from the open models that have been measured. If each image used 0.63 to 2.9 Wh, as measured open models do, the week would total about 440 to 2,000 MWh, with a middle estimate of about 850 MWh. On the world grid's average of 473 g/kWh, the middle case is about 400 tonnes of CO2. Data centres worldwide used about 485 TWh in 2025, roughly 9.3 TWh a week, so the middle case is about 0.01% of a week. All of this is Hum's estimate, not a measurement.

questions.q: Is AI art better for the climate than a human artist drawing the same picture?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A 2024 Scientific Reports study made headlines like 'AI-Driven Creators Are Better For The Environment Than Humans' (Tom's Hardware, https://tomshardware.com/news/ai-driven-creators-are-better-for-the-environment-than-humans-says-new-study), and UC Irvine asked 'Should we let AI take our jobs if it generates less carbon?' (https://ics.uci.edu/2024/01/16/should-we-let-ai-take-our-jobs-if-it-generates-less-carbon-anthropocene/).
questions.verdict: One study says AI emits hundreds to thousands of times less CO2 per picture. The result depends on counting the human's whole daily footprint, so it is a framing choice more than a direct measurement.
questions.answer: Tomlinson and colleagues estimated that an AI image emits 310 to 2,900 times less CO2e than a human illustrator. Midjourney came out about 2,900 times lower than a US artist and 370 times lower than an artist in India. The human side was calculated as the hours spent drawing multiplied by that person's average daily emissions. That counts their whole life footprint, which mostly continues whether or not they draw. The study is an estimate built on assumptions, and its authors say it leaves out job displacement, legal questions and rebound effects. Rebound means people making far more images because AI makes it easy.

questions.q: How much water does it take to make one AI image?
questions.evidence_people_ask: 2026 news on the AI '80s portrait trend claims about 29 mL (two tablespoons) of water per image (Kathmandu Post, https://kathmandupost.com/climate-environment/2026/09/15/the-80s-are-trending-but-ai-nostalgia-comes-with-a-hidden-environmental-cost).
questions.verdict: Probably a few millilitres, most of it at the power station rather than the data centre. Nobody has measured it directly.
questions.answer: No company or study has measured water per image, so this is Hum's estimate. One image takes about 1.22 Wh. Data-centre cooling uses 0.12 to 1.08 litres per kWh, which works out to about 0.15 to 1.3 mL per image on site. Making the electricity also uses water: the US average is 2.18 L/kWh, or about 2.7 mL more. That puts the total at roughly 3 to 4 mL, less than a teaspoon. The real number depends on the site's cooling, its climate and the local power mix. We could not trace the widely shared figure of 29 mL per image to a source that measured images.

questions.q: Which uses more energy overall: training an AI model or people using it (inference)?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A Motley Fool forum thread called 'AI Power Consumption' asks whether running GPT-4 at scale takes as much compute as training it (https://discussion.fool.com/t/ai-power-consumption/108850). Virginia Tech IT's AI environmental-impact page is built around the question of whether training or everyday use is the bigger footprint (https://it.aad.vt.edu/ai/issues/environmental-impact/).
questions.verdict: Over a model's lifetime, using it (inference) now takes most of the energy. Training is a large one-off cost.
questions.answer: Training happens once per model. Inference happens every time anyone uses it. The few companies that have published a split give inference the bigger share. Google said its machine-learning energy split was about 3/5 inference and 2/5 training (company figure, 2019-2021). AWS estimated inference at 80-90% of machine-learning cloud demand, and Meta put about one-third of its ML carbon footprint on inference. MIT Technology Review reports estimates that 80-90% of AI computing power now goes to inference. These numbers measure different things (energy, compute, carbon) and come from company disclosures and estimates, not an independent audit. No regulator publishes an industry-wide split.

questions.q: How much electricity did it take to train GPT-4?

questions.answer: OpenAI has not published GPT-4's training energy, so every figure is an outside estimate. MIT Technology Review reports that training GPT-4 consumed 50 gigawatt-hours, enough to power San Francisco for three days. Divided by the average US home's use (10,791 kWh a year in 2022, EIA), that is about 4,600 homes' electricity for a year. That is our arithmetic on an estimate, not a measurement. The figure is electricity consumed by the computers and data centre. It does not cover the many experimental runs before the final one or the manufacturing of the chips. Newer frontier models are believed to need more, but their training energy is also undisclosed.

questions.q: Meta says training Llama produced zero emissions. How can that be?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Third-party model catalogues (NVIDIA NIM, Azure AI) reprint Meta's '0 tons market-based' line, and a compliance-analysis site notes the zero rests on renewable-matching claims that are not independently verified (https://conductatlas.com/platform/meta/llama-4-model-card/greenhouse-gas-emissions-and-energy-disclosure/). questions.verdict: The zero is an accounting choice (market-based, using renewable purchases). At the grid's actual average it was 11,390 tonnes.
questions.answer: Meta reports two numbers for the same training. Location-based counts emissions at the average carbon of the grids the data centres draw from: 11,390 tonnes CO2eq for Llama 3.1, 1,999 tonnes for Llama 4. Market-based subtracts electricity matched with renewable-energy purchases and certificates, and Meta reports 0 tonnes for both. The electricity the computers consumed is the same either way, and the grid still had to generate it at that moment. Both numbers are company claims. Hum uses location-based figures, because they describe the physical grid.

questions.q: How many chatbot answers add up to the energy of training the model?

questions.verdict: Hundreds of millions to tens of billions of answers. A popular chatbot can get there in days or weeks.
questions.answer: Studies that measured both sides find that inference catches up with training after hundreds of millions of uses. For the BLOOMz models it took about 200 million inferences for the smallest and over 590 million for the largest. Ai2 found hundreds of millions to tens of billions for its OLMo models. Using Mistral's own lifecycle figures, 20,400 tonnes CO2e for training divided by 1.14 g per 400-token answer comes to about 18 billion answers (our arithmetic on company claims). For a service answering billions of prompts a day, the training cost is soon outweighed by use.

questions.q: How much power does a frontier AI training run draw, and is it growing?
questions.evidence_people_ask: News coverage of Epoch AI and EPRI's forecast ran under headlines such as 'AI model training could consume 4 gigawatts by 2030' (https://getcoai.com/news/ai-model-training-could-consume-4-gigawatts-by-2030/). Dror Poleg's data dashboard charts frontier training power for general readers (https://data.drorpoleg.com/charts/frontier-power/).
questions.verdict: The biggest runs now draw over 100 MW. Epoch AI forecasts 4-16 GW per run by 2030, a projection rather than a measurement.
questions.answer: Epoch AI, working with the US Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI), finds that the power drawn by the largest training runs has grown about 2.2 times a year, and the largest runs now exceed 100 megawatts. Their forecast is that the largest single runs in 2030 will likely draw 4-16 gigawatts, comparable to several large power stations. That is a forecast based on the compute trend, not a measured value. For a disclosed example, Meta's Llama 3.1 used 39.3 million H100 GPU-hours. At the chips' 700 W rating that is at most about 27.5 GWh for the GPUs alone, roughly 2,500 US homes' annual electricity (our arithmetic). Cooling and other servers add to it.

questions.q: Why do AI training runs worry grid operators if they're 'only' one-off jobs?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The Register's forums discuss AI power draw (https://forums.theregister.com/post/reply/5214925). Epoch/EPRI's paper was written with a power-industry research institute because utilities are asking how to plan for these loads (https://epoch.ai/publications/power-demands-of-frontier-ai-training).
questions.audience: Energy-curious adults, local residents near data centres
questions.verdict: Because their power use is huge, concentrated in one place, and can swing sharply within minutes.
questions.answer: A training run keeps thousands of chips busy for weeks or months in one place, and the power draw is not smooth. Ai2 measured its own runs swinging between about 15% and 85% of the hardware's maximum draw, with sharp dips whenever the job saves a checkpoint. A load of over 100 MW (Epoch AI's estimate for today's largest runs) jumping up and down like that is something a local grid has to follow in real time. Inference is spread across many data centres and follows users' daily patterns. Grid operators have published little measured data on how these swings affect their systems.

questions.q: Is the footprint of training just the electricity, or do the chips count too?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Coverage of the 'carbon footprint of GPT-4' estimates (https://towardsdatascience.com/the-carbon-footprint-of-gpt-4-d6c676eb21ae) prompts the follow-up of whether hardware is included. Mistral's own release frames its lifecycle analysis as answering this (https://mistral.ai/news/our-contribution-to-a-global-environmental-standard-for-ai).
questions.verdict: Chips and servers add a lot. For BLOOM, counting them roughly doubled the training footprint.
questions.answer: Most published training figures count only the electricity used during the final run. The BLOOM study counted more. Electricity alone came to about 24.7 tonnes CO2eq, and including equipment manufacturing, idle machines and other processes brought it to 50.5 tonnes, roughly double. Mistral's lifecycle analysis says the embodied impacts of its GPUs are a significant portion of the total, without giving a percentage. Ai2 found that the development runs before the final model added about half again on top of the final training. So one 'training run' number usually understates the full cost of making a model.

questions.q: Is it greener to run AI on my phone instead of using ChatGPT in the cloud?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Fediverse thread where a user asks whether running a chatbot locally is justified given the extra power, and Simon Willison replies that hosted LLMs are more efficient: https://friends.grishka.me/posts/2296308 . Axios and Qualcomm coverage of 'moving AI to phones cuts power' (2025) shows this is a live public debate.
questions.audience: Phone owners curious whether 'on-device AI' is the eco option
questions.verdict: Not clearly. Studies disagree, and the answer depends on whether the cloud servers are well run.
questions.answer: Two recent studies point in opposite directions. A 2026 study of 18 models on a Pixel 8 and iPhone 14 found phones about 3 times less energy-efficient per token than a busy server that batches many users together. Counting the carbon from making the phone, it put a phone token at 5 to 7 times the CO2 (an estimate). A 2025 study (SIGMETRICS, promoted by Qualcomm) found a Galaxy S24 used up to 95% less energy. But it compared against cloud servers it calls 'non-optimized'. The same 2026 paper found an unbatched server uses 5.4 times more energy per token than a batched one. Big providers batch, and Google reports a data-centre overhead (PUE) of 1.09.

questions.q: How much battery does one AI answer generated on my phone use?

questions.verdict: Roughly a quarter to three-quarters of 1% of a full charge per answer, in one lab test.
questions.answer: Greenspector, a French measurement firm, tested small models on a Pixel 8 in 2025. Each answer was about 170 tokens. With llama.cpp, one answer used 11 mAh (Llama 3.2 1B) to 34 mAh (Qwen 2.5 7B). The Pixel 8's battery is typically 4,575 mAh, so that is about 0.24% to 0.74% of a full charge. Put another way, a full charge would cover roughly 135 to 415 such answers and nothing else. One model measured 0.11 Wh per answer. That is the phone's own energy use. It is not directly comparable to Google's 0.24 Wh per Gemini prompt, which is a much larger model and includes data-centre overhead.

questions.q: Does Apple Intelligence drain my iPhone battery?

questions.verdict: Nobody has published a measurement. The complaints are real, but they are anecdotes.
questions.answer: Many users report faster drain after turning on Apple Intelligence or updating iOS. Reports blame background work such as indexing photos and summarising notifications. Apple has not published battery figures for these features, and we found no independent lab test of them. Apple says its on-device model has about 3 billion parameters, similar in size to the models Greenspector tested. On a Pixel 8 those used about 0.24% to 0.74% of the battery per answer. That suggests occasional use costs little, while constant background work could add up. Heavy drain right after an update is often temporary indexing.

questions.verdict: Both. A small model runs on the device, and harder requests go to Apple's servers.
questions.answer: Apple describes two models. One has about 3 billion parameters and runs on the phone or Mac. A larger one runs on Apple-silicon servers called Private Cloud Compute. Apple says Apple Intelligence sometimes needs to 'enlist help' from bigger cloud models. Apple decides which requests leave the device, and it has not said what share does. So some Apple Intelligence use adds to data-centre electricity, and some uses your battery. Neither has been published in watt-hours.

questions.q: If I run a chatbot on my own gaming PC, does it use more electricity than ChatGPT?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Fediverse post: a user measured ~120 W from GPT4All and asked 'Do I want to use 6x the energy in my daily PC use?'; Simon Willison replied hosted LLMs should be more efficient: https://friends.grishka.me/posts/2296308
questions.audience: PC gamers and hobbyists running local models (Ollama, LM Studio, GPT4All)
questions.verdict: Usually yes, per answer. A home graphics card serves only you, and data centres share hardware across many users.
questions.answer: One hobbyist test on two RTX 3090 cards (2024) found the best setting used 12.1 joules per token on a 13B model. For a 500-token answer, that is about 1.7 Wh. Published cloud figures are 0.24 Wh (Google) and 0.34 Wh (OpenAI) per text prompt. Those are company claims for typical prompts. The tester noted big operators report 4 to 5 joules per token on far larger models. Another user saw their PC draw about 120 W while generating, roughly 6 times its idle power. Data centres batch many users onto one chip, and a home GPU cannot. These are single-user measurements, not a controlled study.

questions.q: Will AI moving onto phones and laptops mean we need fewer data centres?
questions.evidence_people_ask: UK government AI Energy Council minutes (30 June 2025) record discussion and disagreement on how much AI compute will shift to the edge: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-energy-council-meetings-minutes/ai-energy-council-minutes-monday-30-june-2025-html
questions.verdict: Some, but nobody has put a number on it, and the forecasts still show data centres growing fast.
questions.answer: At the UK's AI Energy Council in 2025, members broadly agreed that some AI computing will move from data centres to devices ('the edge'). They disagreed on how much, and how soon. The IEA told the same meeting that inference, meaning answering requests rather than training models, will be the main driver of AI energy use. The IEA forecast that Hum uses still has data-centre electricity consumption roughly doubling to about 950 TWh by 2030. Phones also hand harder tasks to the cloud, as Apple's Private Cloud Compute does. We found no published estimate of how much demand on-device AI removes.

questions.audience: Readers who have heard AI 'drinks water'
questions.verdict: Probably less water per answer, because a phone needs no cooling water. But the one study is small and promoted by a chipmaker.
questions.answer: Data centres use water for cooling on site, and power plants use water to generate electricity. A phone only has the second kind, through the electricity that charges it. A 2025 study (Li, Islam and Ren) compared a Galaxy S24 with cloud GPUs and found on-device average water savings of up to 96%. That counted cooling plus electricity-generation water for the cloud, and only generation water for the phone. Qualcomm, which promoted the study, notes it was small and used non-optimized cloud servers. Hum already holds the cloud water ranges: 0.12 to 1.08 L/kWh on site and 2.18 L/kWh at US power plants.

questions.verdict: The '10x' figure is from 2023. Newer company figures put a typical text prompt at about what Google said a search used in 2009, but no current figure for a search exists.
questions.answer: The '10x' compared an estimated 3 Wh per ChatGPT request (Alex de Vries, 2023) with Google's own 2009 figure of 0.3 Wh (0.0003 kWh) per search. Newer numbers are much lower. Epoch AI estimates about 0.3 Wh for a typical GPT-4o query. OpenAI says the average is 0.34 Wh, and Google says its median Gemini text prompt uses 0.24 Wh. Both are company claims that no one has checked independently. Those prompts now look similar to the 2009 search figure. But search has almost certainly become more efficient since 2009, and Google hasn't published a new figure, so today's real ratio is unknown. Long answers and reasoning models use more.

questions.q: Do Google's AI Overviews make every search use more energy?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Viral 2024 coverage: 'Google's AI search summaries use 10x more energy than just doing a normal Google search' https://boingboing.net/2024/06/28/googles-ai-search-summaries-use-10x-more-energy-than-just-doing-a-normal-google-search.html
questions.verdict: Almost certainly some more, but Google has not published how much, and outside estimates disagree widely.
questions.answer: An AI summary means running a language model on top of the normal search, so it adds energy. How much is not public. One 2024 preprint by Wim Vanderbauwhede estimated that AI answers raise search energy 60 to 70 times. It used older open models (BLOOM, GPT-3) as stand-ins, and it is an outside estimate, not a measurement. Google's own published figure, 0.24 Wh, is for a median Gemini app text prompt, not for an AI Overview. Google also hasn't published a current figure for a plain search. Until it does, any 'times more' number for AI Overviews is a guess.

figures.quote: energy demand increase by 60-70 times
figures.publisher: Wim Vanderbauwhede, arXiv preprint 'Estimating the Increase in Emissions caused by AI-augmented Search'
figures.check_note: Abstract says 'By our estimates, energy demand increase by 60-70 times.' The low/high values match. The BLOOM/GPT-3 basis was not checked.

figures.quote: we estimate the median Gemini Apps text prompt uses 0.24 watt-hours (Wh) of energy
figures.check_note: Quote matches exactly: 0.24 Wh.

gaps: No Google-published energy figure for an AI Overview.
No current Google-published figure for a conventional search.
The 60-70x estimate is a non-peer-reviewed preprint that relies on older, less efficient models; I could not verify the separate de Vries '10x' AI-search estimate on its primary page.

questions.q: Is asking ChatGPT a question worse than streaming Netflix?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Repeated online comparisons that disagree wildly, from '5.1 seconds of Netflix' (Simon Willison) to '300 to 3000 prompts per hour' (Warp News); a Tildes thread 'Is green AI even possible' debates it. https://simonwillison.net/2025/Nov/29/chatgpt-netflix ; https://tildes.net/~tech/1rjp/is_green_ai_even_possible
questions.verdict: Using company figures, one text prompt uses about as much electricity as 10 to 16 seconds of streaming video.
questions.answer: The IEA's updated estimate for an hour of Netflix in 2019 is about 0.077 kWh, or 77 Wh, and 36 g of CO2. By that measure, OpenAI's 0.34 Wh per query equals about 16 seconds of streaming, and Google's 0.24 Wh equals about 11 seconds. Google itself says 'less than nine seconds' of TV. The comparison isn't quite like for like. 72% of streaming energy is your own screen, while the AI figures count only the data-centre side. And the widely shared claim of 3.2 kg of CO2 per hour of streaming was wrong. The Shift Project later corrected it.

questions.q: Is a video call with my camera on bad for the climate?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Widely shared 2021 advice to 'turn off your Zoom video and help the planet' (Mail & Guardian), repeated by university sustainability blogs. https://mg.co.za/environment/2021-02-28-turn-off-your-zoom-video-and-help-the-planet/
questions.verdict: The estimates disagree by more than tenfold. The most-quoted study gives a high range, and IEA figures for video streaming are far lower.
questions.answer: A 2021 Purdue-led study estimated that an hour of videoconferencing or streaming emits 150 to 1,000 g of CO2 and uses 2 to 12 litres of water, and said that turning the camera off cuts that by 96%. The IEA's estimate for an hour of streamed video in 2019 is much lower, at 36 g of CO2. The gap comes from method. Studies that apply an average energy per gigabyte to network traffic give big numbers, but networks use much of their power whether or not your video is on. Turning the camera off does cut the data sent. How much energy that actually saves is uncertain.

figures.check_note: Exact phrase is on the page: 150 to 1,000 g.

figures.quote: requires 2-12 liters of water
figures.check_note: Exact phrase is on the page: 2 to 12 liters.

figures.check_note: Exact phrase is on the page: 96%.

figures.check_note: Quote matches: 36gCO2.

questions.q: What is the carbon footprint of an email, and should I stop sending 'thank you' emails?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A 2019 OVO Energy claim that one fewer 'thank you' email a day per UK adult would save 16,433 tonnes of carbon a year went viral (Statista chart, WEF repost). https://statista.com/chart/20189/the-carbon-footprint-of-thank-you-emails
questions.verdict: A short email's footprint is tiny, and the famous '4 g per email' comes from a 2010 back-of-envelope estimate that its own author has since cut.
questions.answer: The often-quoted 4 g of CO2e per ordinary email comes from the 2010 edition of Mike Berners-Lee's book How Bad Are Bananas? The 2020 edition is reported to give 0.2 to 0.3 g for a short email and 17 g for a long one. Those figures count a share of everything involved: laptops, Wi-Fi, networks, data centres. Most of that runs whether or not you hit send. As Bristol University's Chris Preist puts it, 'a lot of the system will still have impact, whether or not the email is sent.' Berners-Lee himself calls the footprint of an email 'trivial'.

figures.quote: 4 g CO2e
figures.publisher: Carbon Literacy Project (citing How Bad Are Bananas?, 2010 ed.)
figures.check_note: Page says 'A standard email: 4 g CO2e'. The figure is from the 2010 edition of How Bad are Bananas, and the page warns it is outdated.

figures.quote: The 2020 edition of the same book gives 0.2 to 0.3 g for a short email and 17 g for a long one
figures.publisher: Projet Celsius (secondary, citing Carbon Literacy Project)
figures.check_note: Exact sentence is on the page. Low 0.2 and high 17 match.

figures.quote: The reality is that a lot of the system will still have impact, whether or not the email is sent
figures.publisher: MobileSyrup (quoting Chris Preist, University of Bristol)
figures.check_note: Quote is on the page: Prof Chris Preist (University of Bristol), quoted from the BBC.

figures.quote: the carbon footprint of sending an email is trivial
figures.check_note: Quote is on the page, but it is Mike Berners-Lee's tweet quoted in the article, not the article author's own words. The claim's attribution should be fixed.

questions.q: Will deleting old emails and photos really save water during a drought?
questions.evidence_people_ask: In August 2025 the UK government's National Drought Group told households to delete old emails and pictures; it was widely covered and even used in an English-learning lesson for schools. https://www.gov.uk/government/news/national-drought-group-meets-to-address-nationally-significant-water-shortfall ; https://breakingnewsenglish.com/2508/250818-data-centres-water-r.html
questions.verdict: There is no evidence it saves a meaningful amount, and deleting things uses a little energy too.
questions.answer: The UK advice said to 'delete old emails and pictures as data centres require vast amounts of water to cool their systems.' But storing a file that just sits there takes very little energy. Data centres mostly use water to cool the computers that are busy working, not idle storage. The engineering writer Nick Flaherty pointed out that stored emails sit on air-cooled disk drives, and deleting them uses a processor too. A 2022 Quebec study, as reported, found that deleting 1,000 emails would save only about 5 g of CO2. No one has published how much water deleting a file saves, and UK data-centre water use is not measured nationally.

figures.check_note: Exact sentence is in the 'How to save water at home' list.

figures.claim: Stored data sits on air-cooled drives
figures.quote: Those old emails and pictures are stored on disk drives that use air cooling.
figures.check_note: Exact sentence is on the page.

figures.claim: Deletion itself uses energy
figures.quote: The act of deleting them will use a processor that will use more energy.
figures.check_note: Exact sentence is on the page.

figures.quote: deleting 1,000 emails would only save 5 grams of C02
figures.check_note: Quote is on the page (the source writes 'C02'), credited to a 2022 study by Quebec researchers.

gaps: No published figure for water saved per gigabyte deleted.
UK national data-centre water use is not published; the claim that it is unknown comes from news summaries I could not fetch (DCD returned 403).
The original 2022 Quebec study was not located; the 5 g figure is secondhand.

questions.q: Does gaming use more electricity than AI?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Recurring Reddit arguments comparing gamers' power use with AI users' (subreddit snapshot, April 2026); Andy Masley's widely shared 'cheat sheet' compares ChatGPT with everyday activities. https://reddit.sentinel-team.org/posts/1scfdew/snapshots/2026-04-09T18%3A10%3A25.02225Z ; https://andymasley.substack.com/p/a-cheat-sheet-for-conversations-about
questions.verdict: Per person, a gaming PC uses far more electricity than a typical chatbot user. In total, AI data centres are bigger and growing much faster.
questions.answer: Berkeley Lab estimated that US gaming uses about 34 TWh a year, 2.4% of US home electricity, with about 24 Mt of CO2 a year. A typical gaming PC uses about 1,400 kWh a year, the same as roughly 4 million text prompts at OpenAI's 0.34 Wh each, or about 11,000 a day. But the world's data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, and AI is the fastest-growing part. These numbers aren't strictly comparable. The gaming figures are US-only and several years old, and they count consumption at home.

questions.q: Is cloud gaming worse for the planet than playing on a console or PC?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Consumer and news explainers such as 'Is cloud gaming bad for the environment?' and SCMP's 'Cloud gaming PlayStation titles generates more carbon emissions'. https://www.greengeeks.com/blog/cloud-gaming-bad-environment/ ; https://amp.scmp.com/abacus/games/article/3103488/cloud-gaming-playstation-titles-generates-more-carbon-emissions
questions.verdict: Usually yes. Berkeley Lab found that cloud gaming adds hundreds of watts per player in data centres and networks.
questions.answer: Berkeley Lab calculated that cloud gaming on a PC adds about 340 W per player in the data centre plus 180 W in the network. For console-style cloud gaming it's 180 W plus 120 W. That's on top of your own screen and device. One hour of PC cloud gaming adds about 520 Wh, the same as roughly 1,500 text prompts at 0.34 Wh each. In the most extreme cases, the lab found cloud gaming used up to three times the energy of comparable local play. An industry alliance, Playing for the Planet, puts the average across all kinds of play at about 50 g of CO2e per hour.

questions.q: Does AI now use more electricity than bitcoin mining?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A Simon Fraser University academic's blog answers the question 'Which uses more electricity, AI or crypto?' directly (https://www.sfu.ca/~lmarks/blog/files/38f6a7481e13de4b5ce051ff27804e21-31.html). Many news stories carry the same question, e.g. Decrypt's 'AI's Power Consumption Will Dwarf Bitcoin by Year's End, Says Study' (https://decrypt.co/323320/ai-power-consumption-dwarf-bitcoin-study).
questions.verdict: Probably yes by now, but both numbers are estimates and neither is measured directly.
questions.answer: Bitcoin mining uses roughly 138 to 204 TWh a year. Cambridge's 2025 industry survey estimates 138 TWh, about 0.5% of world electricity. Digiconomist's model gives 204 TWh. A May 2025 peer-reviewed estimate by Alex de Vries-Gao, built from AI chip production numbers, forecast that AI's power demand could reach 23 GW by the start of 2026, about 201 TWh a year. That would put AI on par with or above bitcoin's 176 TWh. All data centres together used about 485 TWh in 2025 (IEA), roughly three times bitcoin. AI companies don't publish AI-only electricity figures, so the AI side is inferred from chip supply, not metered.

figures.quote: 138 TWh (terawatt-hours), or about 0.5% of global consumption
figures.publisher: Cambridge Judge Business School (Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance)
figures.check_note: Cambridge JBS page: 'estimates Bitcoin's annual electricity consumption at 138 TWh (terawatt-hours), or about 0.5% of global consumption'. Mid 138 matches.

figures.claim: Bitcoin annualised electricity consumption, Digiconomist model (live index, read Oct 2026)
figures.check_note: Digiconomist live index currently shows annualized consumption '204.44 TWh' (comparable to Thailand). Live value, so it will drift.

figures.quote: AI's power demand could hit 23 gigawatts by January 1, equivalent to about 201 terawatt-hours annually.
figures.check_note: Decrypt quotes the line verbatim: 23 GW by January 1, about 201 TWh annually. 23 GW x 8760 h = 201.5 TWh, consistent.

figures.claim: Bitcoin consumption used as the comparison in the same article
figures.quote: Bitcoin currently consumes around 176 TWh per year.
figures.check_note: Decrypt: 'Bitcoin currently consumes around 176 TWh per year.' Matches.

figures.claim: All data centres (IEA, 485 TWh in 2025, already in Hum) divided by Cambridge's bitcoin estimate: 485 / 138 = about 3.5 times
figures.quote: 138 TWh (terawatt-hours), or about 0.5% of global consumption
figures.check_note: Derived figure. The 138 TWh quote is on the Cambridge page. 485/138 = 3.51, so ~3.5 is correct. The 485 TWh comes from IEA (already in Hum) and was not checked here.

questions.q: How much of America's electricity goes to bitcoin mining compared with data centres?
questions.evidence_people_ask: EIA wrote an explainer and ran an emergency survey after public and congressional concern about crypto loads (https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=61364). The question also comes up in many news stories on US grid strain.
questions.verdict: Bitcoin mining is an estimated 0.6% to 2.3% of US electricity. Data centres were about 4.4% in 2023.
questions.answer: In February 2024, the US Energy Information Administration estimated that US bitcoin mining used 25 to 91 TWh a year, which is 0.6% to 2.3% of US electricity consumption. This is a top-down estimate: Cambridge's global index multiplied by an assumed ~38% US share. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory puts US data centres at about 176 TWh, or 4.4%, in 2023, and forecasts 6.7% to 12% by 2028. So data centres were roughly two to seven times bitcoin mining in the US, and data centres are the part that is growing fastest. EIA has stopped its emergency survey of miners, so there is no newer official US figure.

figures.quote: we estimate electricity usage from Bitcoin mining based in the United States to range from 25 TWh to 91 TWh.
figures.check_note: EIA page quote is verbatim: 25 TWh to 91 TWh.

figures.quote: annual electricity use from cryptocurrency mining probably represents from 0.6% to 2.3% of U.S. electricity consumption.
figures.check_note: Exact summary sentence is on the EIA page: 'probably represents from 0.6% to 2.3% of U.S. electricity consumption.' Also restated as a share of 2023 US demand (3,900 TWh).

figures.check_note: LBNL news release: 'Data centers consumed about 4.4% of total U.S. electricity in 2023'.

figures.quote: are expected to consume between 6.7 and 12% of total U.S. electricity by 2028.
figures.check_note: LBNL: 'are expected to consume between 6.7 and 12% of total U.S. electricity by 2028'. Low/high match.

figures.check_note: Derived. EIA 25-91 TWh quote confirmed. LBNL page confirms 176 TWh in 2023. 176/91 = 1.93 and 176/25 = 7.04, so 1.9x to 7x is correct.

questions.q: Is one bitcoin transaction really worse than thousands of ChatGPT questions?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Decrypt reported on a crypto-industry argument that per-query AI energy claims mirror per-transaction bitcoin claims ('AI Energy FUD Is The New Bitcoin Mining FUD', https://decrypt.co/200007/artificial-intelligence-energy-consumption-versus-bitcoin-mining). Fediverse and Lemmy threads also compare the two (https://lemmy.4d2.org/post/2904533/3886388).
questions.verdict: On paper one transaction equals millions of prompts, but per-transaction is a shaky way to measure bitcoin.
questions.answer: Digiconomist estimates about 759 kWh per bitcoin transaction. That is about 26 days of an average US household's electricity. Divided by OpenAI's stated 0.34 Wh per ChatGPT prompt, it comes to about 2.2 million prompts. Treat that comparison with care. Bitcoin's electricity is spent on mining, which runs whatever the number of transactions, so dividing it by transactions gives a big but fragile number. Crypto commentators make the same complaint about per-query AI figures. A fairer comparison is total yearly electricity: bitcoin roughly 138 to 204 TWh, all data centres about 485 TWh in 2025.

questions.q: Is bitcoin mining greener or dirtier than AI data centres?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Cambridge's 2025 survey on the share of sustainable energy in mining got wide coverage, including framing around Elon Musk's 50% threshold for Tesla accepting bitcoin again (https://www.theblock.co/news/business/2025-04-29-cambridge-university-bitcoin-mining-sustainable-energy-use-elon-musk-tesla-btc-payments-352332).
questions.verdict: Unclear. Miners say about half their power is renewable or nuclear, and estimates of bitcoin's CO2 range from 40 to 114 Mt.
questions.answer: Cambridge's 2025 survey of 49 mining firms found 52.4% of bitcoin mining electricity came from renewables plus nuclear. Natural gas, at 38.2%, is now the single largest source. It estimates network emissions at 39.8 Mt CO2e a year. Digiconomist's model gives a much higher 114 Mt CO2. For comparison, the IEA puts all data centres at about 180 Mt CO2 today. The survey covers firms reporting about 48% of mining and is self-reported, so it is a company-sourced estimate, not a measurement. No source gives a like-for-like energy mix for AI alone, so a clean 'greener' verdict isn't possible.

figures.check_note: Cambridge: 'The use of sustainable energy sources for Bitcoin mining has grown to 52.4%'.

figures.check_note: Cambridge: 'natural gas, at 38.2% (up from 25.0% in 2022)'. Verbatim.

figures.quote: corresponding network-wide emissions at 39.8 MtCO2e

questions.q: Why are bitcoin mines turning into AI data centres?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Widely covered in tech and business news, e.g. TechRadar 'Is AI more appealing than crypto now? A major Bitcoin miner has decided to pivot to AI data centers' (https://www.techradar.com/pro/is-ai-more-appealing-than-crypto-now-a-major-bitcoin-miner-has-decided-to-pivot-to-ai-data-centers-heres-why) and Bisnow (https://www.bisnow.com/news/national/data-center/ai-is-pushing-big-tech-and-bitcoin-data-centers-closer-together-124505).

questions.verdict: Because the scarce thing for AI is a ready grid connection, and miners already have one.
questions.answer: New data centres often wait years for a grid connection. Bitcoin miners already hold sites with large power hookups, so AI companies lease or buy them. Bisnow reported grid waits of up to seven years and developers willing to build 'anywhere' they can find hundreds of megawatts. Core Scientific, once a big miner, reports more than 1,300 MW of contracted power and now mainly hosts AI. CoreWeave's planned $9 billion takeover was voted down by Core Scientific shareholders in October 2025, but the leasing deal continues. A switch like this doesn't cut grid demand. The same megawatts move from mining to AI.

Mining can stop with little loss because a paused machine only misses bitcoin rewards. AI training and live chat services are generally run continuously. questions.q: Didn't Ethereum fix crypto's energy problem? Could AI do something similar?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The Merge is a common answer in arguments over 'crypto is bad for the planet', and ethereum.org keeps a dedicated FAQ page on energy consumption (https://ethereum.org/en/energy-consumption/) because the question keeps coming up.
questions.verdict: Ethereum cut its electricity use by about 99.99% by dropping mining. AI has no equivalent switch.
questions.answer: In 2022 Ethereum moved from proof-of-work mining to proof-of-stake ('The Merge'). A Crypto Carbon Ratings Institute estimate quoted by ethereum.org says annual electricity fell by more than 99.988%, from about 21 TWh a year to about 0.0026 TWh. That was possible because mining was the energy-hungry part, and proof-of-stake doesn't need it. Bitcoin still uses proof-of-work. AI is different. The electricity goes into the computing that is the product itself, so efficiency gains come from better chips and models, and growing use tends to eat those gains. These Ethereum figures come from the project's own site, citing CCRI.

questions.q: Is one AI chatbot question really like boiling a kettle?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The kettle comparison keeps coming up in articles and blogs, e.g. a Medium piece calling a ChatGPT query '3% of boiling a kettle' (https://medium.com/illumination/how-much-energy-exactly-does-chatgpt-use-0a0bdf2e4cd4). News coverage of OpenAI's figure framed it with household appliances too (https://www.yahoo.com/news/one-chatgpt-query-uses-same-093126817.html).
questions.audience: Everyday adults who have heard 'one prompt = a kettle' type claims
questions.verdict: No. By the companies' own figures, one text prompt uses a few hundred times less energy than boiling a litre of water.
questions.answer: Physics sets the floor for a kettle. Heating 1 litre of water from 15 C to 100 C takes about 99 Wh, and real kettles lose a little more. OpenAI says an average ChatGPT query uses about 0.34 Wh, and Google says a median Gemini text prompt uses 0.24 Wh. Both are company claims that haven't been independently audited. On those numbers, one litre boiled equals roughly 290 to 410 text prompts. The kettle comparison only works for heavy tasks. Generating a short video (around 90 Wh, Hugging Face's estimate, which Hum already holds) is close to one kettle boil.

That number comes from the specific heat of water, not from a lab test of a particular kettle. A full 1.7 L kettle therefore needs at least about 0.17 kWh, and a single 250 mL mug about 0.025 kWh. Real kettles use somewhat more because of heat loss, and we did not find a government-measured efficiency figure. These are amounts of electricity consumed at the plug.

questions.q: How does the CO2 from an AI prompt compare with driving a car one kilometre?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Projet Celsius's FAQ compares a year of chatbot use to driving 20 km (https://projetcelsius.com/en/faq/empreinte-numerique-ia/does-quitting-chatgpt-reduce-your-carbon-footprint/). A Fediverse thread cites the EPA figure of about 400 g CO2 per mile (https://activitypub.space/post/https%3A%2F%2Fcosocial.ca%2Fusers%2Fevan%2Fstatuses%2F115589565464078072). Hannah Ritchie asks 'What's the carbon footprint of using ChatGPT?' (https://hannahritchie.substack.com/p/carbon-footprint-chatgpt).
questions.audience: Adults weighing digital habits against driving
questions.verdict: Driving one kilometre in an average US car emits about as much CO2 as a couple of thousand text prompts.
questions.answer: The US EPA estimates an average passenger vehicle emits 393 g CO2e per mile, about 244 g per km. New EU cars averaged 96.7 g/km in 2025, but that is a lab test-cycle figure (WLTP), not real-world driving. A 0.34 Wh prompt (OpenAI's own claim) on the 2022 US average grid (about 373 g CO2 per kWh generated) comes to roughly 0.13 g. Google claims 0.03 g for its median prompt. So 1 km in an average US car is roughly 1,900 to 8,100 prompts. This leaves out training the models and making the hardware.

questions.verdict: About 39 million average US homes' worth of electricity in 2024, and far more homes in countries that use less per house.

In countries where homes use less (for example a few thousand kWh a year), the same electricity covers many more homes. The IEA projects around 945 TWh by 2030, roughly 89 million US-average homes. That 2030 figure is a forecast.

questions.q: Is an hour of Netflix more energy than asking an AI a question?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The IEA wrote a fact-check because of viral claims about streaming's footprint (https://www.iea.org/commentaries/the-carbon-footprint-of-streaming-video-fact-checking-the-headlines). questions.verdict: Yes. An hour of streaming (2019 IEA estimate) used about as much energy as a couple of hundred text prompts.
questions.answer: The IEA estimated that streaming a Netflix video in 2019 used about 0.077 kWh (77 Wh) per hour, end to end, at about 36 g CO2 per hour. That is roughly 230 text prompts at OpenAI's claimed 0.34 Wh, or about 320 at Google's 0.24 Wh. Google says one median prompt equals 'watching TV for less than nine seconds.' The streaming figure is from 2019, and devices and networks have become more efficient since. A newer IEA figure was not found. Most of the streaming energy is used by the viewer's TV or device, not the data centre.

questions.q: Does a ChatGPT question really use 10 times the energy of a Google search?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Fact-checks and explainers written to answer this exact question, e.g. the Substack post 'Does ChatGPT use 10x more energy than a standard Google search?' (https://engineeringprompts.substack.com/p/does-chatgpt-use-10x-more-energy) and Epoch AI's explainer, which opens with the '10 times as much as a Google search' claim (https://epoch.ai/gradient-updates/how-much-energy-does-chatgpt-use). Andy Masley also says the claim comes up 'at parties' and in popular Twitter posts (https://blog.andymasley.com/p/individual-ai-use-is-not-bad-for).
questions.audience: Everyday ChatGPT users and students who have seen the '10x Google' line on social media
questions.verdict: Probably not any more. The 10x figure came from a 2023 off-the-cuff remark and a 2009 Google number, and newer estimates put a typical text prompt near 0.3 Wh.
questions.answer: The claim has two roots. In 2023 Alphabet's chairman said an AI chat 'likely' cost 10 times a keyword search. Researcher Alex de Vries then paired that with a 2009 Google figure of 0.3 Wh per search, which gives about 3 Wh per AI query. Newer numbers are much lower. Epoch AI estimates about 0.3 Wh for a typical GPT-4o query, OpenAI's CEO says 0.34 Wh, and Google says its median Gemini text prompt uses 0.24 Wh. All three are estimates or company claims, not independent measurements. Nobody has published a current energy figure for a Google search, so the true ratio today is unknown. Long reasoning prompts can use far more.

questions.q: Does ChatGPT drink a bottle of water for every question?
questions.evidence_people_ask: GovTech ran it as a 'Question of the Day': 'How much water does ChatGPT drink for every 20 questions it answers?' (https://www.govtech.com/question-of-the-day/how-much-water-does-chatgpt-drink-for-every-20-questions-it-answers). Euronews headline: 'ChatGPT drinks a bottle of fresh water for every 20 to 50 questions we ask' (https://www.euronews.com/green/2023/04/20/chatgpt-drinks-a-bottle-of-fresh-water-for-every-20-to-50-questions-we-ask-study-warns). Also a 2026 Reddit thread asking how much water and power one chatbot question uses (https://reddit.sentinel-team.org/posts/1u1bbr1/snapshots/2026-06-09T21%3A26%3A38.97698Z).

questions.verdict: No. The original study said one 500 ml bottle per 10 to 50 responses from GPT-3, not per question, and newer company figures are far smaller.
questions.answer: The bottle comes from a 2023 UC Riverside paper. It estimated that GPT-3 'drinks' 500 ml for roughly 10 to 50 medium-length responses, so about 10 to 50 ml each. That count includes water evaporated at power plants as well as cooling water at the data centre. It also assumed 4 Wh of server energy per request, more than ten times what OpenAI now claims. Newer figures are company claims: OpenAI says about 0.32 ml per average query, and Google says 0.26 ml (about five drops) per median Gemini prompt. These may count only on-site water. The answer depends on what you count, where the data centre is, and which model you use.

questions.q: Does writing one email with AI use a whole bottle of water?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The September 2024 Washington Post / UC Riverside graphic spread widely, e.g. Yahoo News 'Using GPT-4 to generate 100 words...' (https://www.yahoo.com/news/using-gpt-4-generate-100-120051801.html) and the AskWoody forum thread 'Send One Email With ChatGPT is the Equivalent of Consuming One Bottle of Water' (https://www.askwoody.com/forums/topic/send-one-email-with-chatgpt-is-the-equivalent-of-consuming-one-bottle-of-water). Andy Masley calls it 'a commonly cited statistic' (https://blog.andymasley.com/p/individual-ai-use-is-not-bad-for).
questions.audience: Office workers using AI to draft email; people who saw the Washington Post chart
questions.verdict: It's an estimate built on older, higher energy assumptions. It also counts water used at power plants and varies about sixfold by US state, so treat it as a ceiling, not a fact.
questions.answer: The figure comes from a 2024 Washington Post analysis with UC Riverside researchers. They modelled GPT-4 writing a 100-word email and estimated a bit over one bottle of water. An email may take several prompts, so the true figure is uncertain.

questions.q: Why do estimates of water per AI prompt differ by a hundred times or more?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Sean Goedecke's widely shared post 'Talking to ChatGPT costs 5ml of water, not 500ml' (https://www.seangoedecke.com/water-impact-of-ai/), and the Projet Celsius FAQ 'Does AI really consume half a litre of water per request?' (https://projetcelsius.com/en/faq/empreinte-numerique-ia/l-ia-consomme-t-elle-vraiment-un-demi-litre-d-eau-par-requet/).

questions.verdict: Different studies count different things: on-site cooling only versus cooling plus power-plant water, old versus new models, and per page versus per chat.
questions.answer: Estimates of water per prompt run from about 50 ml down to about 0.26 ml. Four choices explain most of the gap. Is power-plant water counted, or only cooling water at the data centre? Which model, since newer ones use less energy per answer? Where is the data centre, since climate and grid change the water per kWh? And is the unit a prompt, a page or a whole conversation? The 2023 UC Riverside study counted both kinds of water and assumed 4 Wh per request. Google's 0.26 ml figure is a company claim using its own method. Sean Goedecke argues the old study also confused per-page with per-request. No figure is independently measured.

questions.q: Should I delete old emails and photos to save water?
questions.evidence_people_ask: In August 2025 the UK National Drought Group publicly advised people to delete old emails and pictures (https://www.gov.uk/government/news/national-drought-group-meets-to-address-nationally-significant-water-shortfall). This prompted fact-checks like Black Dot Research's 'Does deleting emails help save water?' (https://blackdotresearch.sg/does-deleting-emails-help-save-water/) and wide coverage (TechRadar, PetaPixel).
questions.audience: UK households during drought; anyone who saw the 'delete your emails' advice
questions.verdict: It makes almost no difference. Stored files sit mostly idle, and the water goes to active computing such as AI and video.
questions.answer: The UK National Drought Group suggested it in 2025, saying data centres need lots of water for cooling. That part is true, but the cooling load comes mainly from active work such as AI requests and video processing, not old files on disks that sit mostly idle. A fact-check by Black Dot Research rated the claim 'partly true'. It found the effect of one person deleting emails 'almost negligible', and noted some experts think hunting through and deleting files could use more energy than leaving them. No official figure exists for how much water deleting saves. Total UK data-centre water use isn't published either.

questions.q: Does training one AI model emit as much CO2 as five cars over their lifetimes?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The 2019 MIT Technology Review headline 'Training a single AI model can emit as much carbon as five cars in their lifetimes' (https://www.technologyreview.com/2019/06/06/239031/training-a-single-ai-model-can-emit-as-much-carbon-as-five-cars-in-their-lifetimes/) is still one of the most-cited AI climate statistics.
questions.audience: Students, journalists, people citing AI's training footprint
questions.verdict: That figure was for an unusual experiment (a big automated model-design search), and Google, which ran the real search, says the estimate was about 88 times too high.
questions.answer: The 2019 University of Massachusetts study estimated that one neural architecture search, an automated trial-and-error hunt for a better model design, could emit over 626,000 pounds of CO2e. That's nearly five times a US car's lifetime emissions. It was not typical model training. In 2022 Google, which ran the actual search, said the study overshot by 88 times: about 3,223 kg CO2e versus the study's 284,019 kg. That is a company claim about its own work. Training today's frontier models is far bigger, and most companies don't publish its energy or emissions.

questions.q: Is watching 30 minutes of Netflix really like driving 4 miles?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A 2019 Shift Project figure repeated by many outlets, which the IEA fact-checked in 'The carbon footprint of streaming video: fact-checking the headlines' (https://www.iea.org/commentaries/the-carbon-footprint-of-streaming-video-fact-checking-the-headlines). It is the template for today's AI per-use myths.
questions.audience: Anyone comparing digital habits to driving; readers of earlier 'digital carbon' headlines
questions.verdict: No. The headline rested on a bits-versus-bytes slip, and the IEA estimated the real impact was up to about 90 times smaller.
questions.answer: In 2019 headlines said half an hour of Netflix emitted 1.6 kg of CO2, like driving almost 4 miles. The IEA's analyst traced the number to a Shift Project calculation that apparently read 3 megabits per second as 3 megabytes per second, an eightfold error. He estimated about 0.077 kWh and 36 g CO2 per hour of streaming in 2019, so about 18 g for half an hour. That is an estimate that depends on the grid and the devices used. It matters for AI because the same pattern repeats: a per-use number goes viral before anyone checks the units.

questions.q: Are data centres using up Arizona's water?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Local TV explainer 'Why do data centers need water' (KGUN 9) and a KJZZ segment titled 'Is there enough water to sustain them'; a change.org petition 'Get data centers out of Arizona'. https://www.kgun9.com/news/local-news/why-do-data-centers-need-water ; https://www.kjzz.org/the-show/2025-04-16/the-valley-is-a-popular-spot-for-data-centers-is-there-enough-water-to-sustain-them ; https://www.change.org/p/get-data-centers-out-of-arizona
questions.audience: Arizona residents, people reading about Colorado River cuts
questions.verdict: Not today by volume: farms use most of Arizona's water, and data-centre cooling is a small slice. But it is growing, and much of the data is hidden.
questions.answer: A Ceres estimate puts Phoenix-area data-centre cooling at about 385 million gallons a year. Counting water at power plants, it reaches 3.3 billion. The cooling figure is about 1,180 acre-feet, around 0.06% of the Colorado River water Arizona expects to use in 2026. Agriculture uses 72% of the state's water. Ceres projects cooling use could grow about tenfold. Arizona State University's Kyl Center disputes parts of the method, and says even the worst case is about 1% of Phoenix-area home water use. The real local worry is that a water provider can promise a share of its supply to one data centre. Google's Mesa permit allows 5.5 million cubic metres a year.

questions.q: How much water do Texas data centres use, and could they run Texas dry?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Texas Standard and High Plains Public Radio coverage, e.g. 'Data centers are thirsty for Texas water but state planners don't know how much they will need'; Austin Chronicle 'Texas is still in drought and AI data centers are quietly guzzling up water'. https://www.hppr.org/hppr-news/2025-09-29/data-centers-are-thirsty-for-texas-water-but-state-planners-dont-know-how-much-they-will-need ; https://www.austinchronicle.com/news/2025-07-25/texas-is-still-in-drought-and-ai-data-centers-are-quietly-guzzling-up-water/
questions.audience: Texans and people following drought news
questions.verdict: About 0.4% of Texas water use in 2025, according to one independent estimate. That could rise to 2.7% by 2030, and the use is clustered in dry areas.
questions.answer: The Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) estimates Texas data centres consumed about 25 billion gallons in 2025. That is roughly 95 billion litres, or 0.4% of the state's water use. The estimate counts both cooling water and water at power plants. If growth forecasts hold, it could reach 29 to 161 billion gallons by 2030, or 0.5% to 2.7% of state use. These are estimates. Texas does not require data centres to report water use, and the state utility regulator only began surveying operators in 2026. The use is concentrated in watersheds that are already stressed. In April 2025, over 80% of Texas was in drought.

questions.q: Is most of a data centre's water used at the building, or at the power plant?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A recurring point in Arizona coverage: KJZZ notes that zero-water cooling needs more energy, and energy is part of the water equation. Reddit-style comment threads ask why data centres don't just stop using water. https://www.kjzz.org/the-show/2025-04-16/the-valley-is-a-popular-spot-for-data-centers-is-there-enough-water-to-sustain-them ; https://piefed.keyboardvagabond.com/post/33556
questions.verdict: In Texas, about two-thirds of it is at the power plants, according to HARC's estimate.
questions.answer: HARC applies Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's US average of 95 gallons per MWh to Texas's 464 data centres. That gives about 8 billion gallons a year of on-site cooling water. The power plants supplying them consume about 17 billion gallons. So roughly 68% is indirect, at the power plant, and 32% is at the building. Power plants also withdraw far more water than they consume, about 1,067 billion gallons, but most of that is returned. 'Consumption' here means water that evaporates and doesn't come back. The split differs by place: solar and wind need almost no cooling water, while coal, gas and nuclear plants do.

figures.quote: At this rate, the 464 data centers in Texas would directly consume 8 Bgal of water (24 kAF) per year for cooling.
figures.check_note: Quote is in the HARC PDF, word for word. 8 Bgal direct cooling per year matches.

figures.claim: LBNL on-site water intensity used by HARC
figures.quote: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates data centers in 2023 consumed 95 gallons per megawatt-hour (MWh).
figures.check_note: Quote is in the HARC PDF, word for word. 95 gal/MWh matches.

figures.claim: Indirect (power-plant) water withdrawn and consumed for Texas data centres' electricity
figures.unit: US gallons per year consumed (withdrawal 1,067 billion)
figures.quote: the grid power supplying the 464 data centers in Texas withdraws about 1,067 Bgal (3.3 mAF) and consumes 17 Bgal (53 kAF) per year.
figures.check_note: Quote is in the HARC PDF, word for word. 17 Bgal consumed and 1,067 Bgal withdrawn match.

figures.claim: Indirect share = 17 / (8 + 17) = 68%; on-site share = 8 / 25 = 32%
figures.unit: % of total consumption at power plants
figures.quote: the grid power supplying the 464 data centers in Texas withdraws about 1,067 Bgal (3.3 mAF) and consumes 17 Bgal (53 kAF) per year.
figures.check_note: Input quote is in the PDF. Derived 17/(8+17) = 68% is correct.

gaps: The split is Texas-specific. Comparable on-site vs power-plant splits for Arizona, Chile, Spain, Uruguay or India were not found.
Using the US-average LBNL intensity for Texas ignores differences in local climate and cooling design.

questions.q: Why did Google change its Uruguay data centre plan during the drought?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The Guardian (July 2023), 'It's pillage: thirsty Uruguayans decry Google's plan to exploit water supply', covered protests in Canelones; campaigners went to court to get Google's water figures. Thomson Reuters Foundation: 'In Latin America, data center plans fuel water worries'. https://www.context.news/big-tech/in-latin-america-data-center-plans-fuel-water-worries
questions.audience: Readers in Latin America, students of the 2023 Montevideo water crisis
questions.verdict: The first design would have used drinking water, as much as 55,000 people use, at the peak of a historic drought. Google shrank the project and switched to air cooling.
questions.answer: Google's early plan for its data centre near Montevideo (in Canelones) would have used up to 7.6 million litres of drinking water a day. That is about what 55,000 Montevideo residents use daily, or roughly 2.8 billion litres a year, and it came during the 2023 drought peak, when tap water turned salty. After protests and a court fight over disclosure, Google made the project smaller and switched to air cooling. It also said the site would use less than 560 GWh of electricity a year. Uruguay's Environment Ministry approved it in 2024. Air cooling shifts the load from water to electricity. The ministry later fought a court order to publish Google's water data, calling it a trade secret.

questions.verdict: A court partly overturned the permit over drought and climate risk, and Google dropped its water-cooled design for air cooling.
questions.answer: Google's original design for Cerrillos, in Santiago, used about 169 litres of fresh water a second for cooling. In February 2024, Chile's environmental court partly overturned the permit and told Google to account for climate change. In September 2024, Google said it would drop the original design and restart with air-cooled chillers. These are design figures from the permit fight, not measured use. The plant had not yet operated with water cooling.

questions.verdict: Hundreds of millions of litres a year per campus are planned or licensed. The published numbers disagree, and actual use is not public.
questions.answer: Meta's planned campus at Talavera de la Reina was reported to need about 660 million litres a year. About 200 million of that is for the data centre and about 440 million for the rest of the site. These are planning figures, in an area at risk of drought. In Aragón, Amazon's three proposed data centres are licensed for about 755,720 cubic metres (756 million litres) a year. Amazon has said its three Aragón centres can use up to 53.9 million litres. Those numbers may cover different things, and Amazon also asked to raise use at existing sites by 48%. In August 2026, Spain's cabinet approved a draft decree setting binding water conditions for new data centres.

questions.answer: Industry estimates put Indian data-centre water use at about 150 billion litres in 2025, possibly 358 billion litres by 2030. These come from consultancy and market-research projections, not official data, and companies don't have to publish actual use. S&P Global forecasts that 60–80% of India's data centres could face high water stress this decade. Karnataka has 32 private data centres, 31 of them in Bengaluru, where aquifers are running low. A figure quoted there of 25 million litres per MW a year works out to about 2.9 litres per kWh. That is above typical on-site cooling rates, so it may include power-plant water or assume a worst case.

questions.q: Do five ChatGPT questions really use half a litre of water?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Karnataka IT Minister Priyank Kharge told the state Assembly in 2026: 'If you ask five questions on ChatGPT, 500 ml of water is needed.' The 'bottle of water' claim also circulates widely online and in schools. https://www.thenewsminute.com/karnataka/in-bengalurus-water-stressed-areas-sit-most-of-its-data-centres
questions.audience: Everyone; especially students and people who've seen the claim on social media
questions.verdict: Probably not. Five questions is a stretch even of the study the claim comes from, and newer company figures are far lower.
questions.answer: The claim traces to a 2023 University of California study. It estimated that GPT-3 'drinks' a 500 ml bottle for every 10 to 50 medium-length responses, depending on when and where it runs, counting power-plant water as well as cooling. That is 10–50 ml per response, so five questions would use 50–250 ml, not 500. In 2025, Google reported its median Gemini text prompt uses 0.26 ml, about five drops. Five prompts would be about 1.3 ml. That is a company figure based on its fleet-average cooling-water rate, so it likely leaves out power-plant water. Newer models and data centres differ, and OpenAI has not published a comparable audited water figure.

questions.q: Can data centres be built to use no water at all?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Commenters on the Tucson data-centre rejection ask why companies don't use dry cooling; Microsoft's 'zero water' design announcement was widely covered (ITPro, ESG Today). https://piefed.keyboardvagabond.com/post/33556 ; https://www.esgtoday.com/microsoft-launches-new-datacenter-design-avoiding-use-of-water-for-cooling
questions.verdict: For cooling, mostly yes, but it costs more electricity, and the power plants still use water.
questions.answer: Closed-loop or air cooling can remove most on-site water use. Microsoft says all its new designs since August 2024 circulate water in a sealed loop. It says this avoids more than 125 million litres a year per data centre, about 50 Olympic pools. Pilots in Phoenix and Wisconsin start in 2026 and come online in late 2027. Google moved its Uruguay and Chile projects to air cooling after drought protests. The trade-off is that mechanical cooling uses more electricity, which Microsoft admits raises its PUE (an energy-efficiency measure). Where power comes from thermal plants, some of the water simply moves to the power station. In Texas, power plants already account for about two-thirds of data centres' water.

questions.q: What is the difference between evaporative and closed-loop cooling in a data centre, and why don't they all use closed loops?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A viewer named Rob asked WKYT's 'Good Question' segment (July 2026) why data centres use so much water. The answer contrasts evaporative and closed-loop cooling. https://www.wkyt.com/2026/07/23/good-question-why-do-data-centers-use-so-much-water/
questions.audience: General adults and students who have heard 'AI drinks water' and want to know how the cooling works
questions.verdict: Evaporating water saves electricity and closed loops save water, so operators trade one against the other.
questions.answer: Evaporative cooling removes heat by letting water evaporate into the air, so that water leaves the site. A closed loop keeps the same water circulating and dumps the heat through chillers or dry coolers, which takes more electricity. The companies quote different sizes for that trade-off. Amazon says chillers typically need 25% to 35% more electricity. Google says water cooling can cut energy use by about 10% compared with air cooling in some regions. Microsoft expects only a 'nominal' fleet-wide energy increase from its new zero-water design. These are company claims, not independent measurements. The extra electricity also uses water at power plants, so a closed loop moves part of the water footprint off-site rather than removing it.

figures.quote: chillers typically require 25% to 35% more electricity
figures.check_note: Quote on the aboutamazon.com page; 25-35% matches.

figures.claim: Google says water cooling can reduce data-centre energy use by about 10% compared with air cooling in some regions
figures.quote: water cooling can reduce data center energy use by roughly 10% compared to air cooling in some regions
figures.check_note: Exact quote on the WaterWorld page; 10% matches.

figures.claim: Microsoft says replacing evaporative cooling with mechanical cooling gives a nominal increase in annual energy use
figures.quote: The result is a nominal increase in our annual energy usage compared to our evaporative datacenter designs across the global fleet.
figures.check_note: Exact sentence in the 2025 Microsoft Environmental Sustainability Report PDF.

gaps: No independent, peer-reviewed figure was found for the electricity penalty of closed-loop versus evaporative cooling across climates.
No source gave the share of the world's data centres using each cooling type. WKYT's 75-90% water-cooled figure comes from a trade association and was not traced to a primary source.

questions.q: If data-centre cooling is a closed loop, how can they 'consume' water at all?
questions.evidence_people_ask: In a Lemmy (Reddit-style) thread, one user argues the cooling is a closed loop so no water is consumed, and others push back. https://lemmy.federate.cc/post/4022819/8471728
questions.audience: Sceptical readers who think the water just goes round and round
questions.verdict: Most of the water taken in evaporates and does not come back. At Google's data centres, about four-fifths of what was withdrawn in 2024 was consumed.
questions.answer: 'Withdrawal' is water taken in. 'Discharge' is water sent back, usually to sewers. 'Consumption' is the difference, mostly water that evaporated in cooling towers. Google publishes all three for each site. In 2024 its data centres withdrew 9,866 million gallons, discharged 2,079 million and consumed 7,787 million. That means about 79% of what came in did not go back (our arithmetic on Google's reported, assured figures). Closed loops do exist, mainly in newer liquid-cooled designs, but most existing evaporative systems lose water to the air by design.

questions.q: Do 'zero-water' data centres, like Microsoft's new design, really use no water?

The WKYT reader question also contrasts closed-loop and evaporative systems. https://www.wkyt.com/2026/07/23/good-question-why-do-data-centers-use-so-much-water/
questions.verdict: They use zero water for cooling on-site, but not zero water overall. The sites are mostly still being built.
questions.answer: Microsoft's design uses direct-to-chip liquid cooling. Water is filled once during construction and then circulated in a closed loop. Restrooms and kitchens still use water. More electricity is needed, and power plants use water too (Hum's US figure is about 2.18 L/kWh generated). The first sites, in Phoenix and Wisconsin, are piloting in 2026 and are due online in late 2027.

questions.q: How much water do US data centres use in total?

questions.verdict: About 17 billion gallons on-site in 2023, plus roughly 12 times that indirectly through the power plants that make their electricity. Both are estimates.
questions.answer: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that US data centres used about 17 billion gallons (about 64 billion litres) of water directly for cooling in 2023. These are modelled estimates, because companies report water use voluntarily and inconsistently. The study also came before the biggest wave of AI construction.

questions.q: Do data centres use drinking water?
questions.evidence_people_ask: An IOL (South Africa) article from February 2026 is headlined 'Why are AI data centres using fresh drinking water instead of recycled water?' https://iol.co.za/news/environment/2026-02-11-why-are-ai-data-centres-using-fresh-drinking-water-instead-of-recycled-water/
questions.audience: Residents near proposed data centres; general adults
questions.verdict: Mostly, yes. Over three-quarters of what Google's data centres drew in 2024 was potable water, though some sites run on reclaimed water.
questions.answer: Google's per-site table gives the source of its water. That makes about 78% potable and 9% reclaimed (our arithmetic). Drinking water is often chosen because it is cheap and clean, so it causes less scale and corrosion in cooling towers. Amazon says it runs 26 facilities on 100% reclaimed water, but it does not publish a fleet-wide share.

questions.q: What is WUE, and how do the big companies compare on water per unit of electricity?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The Conversation explainer notes that each company reports different water statistics, so readers cannot compare them directly. https://aihub.org/2025/09/24/data-centers-consume-massive-amounts-of-water-companies-rarely-tell-the-public-exactly-how-much
questions.verdict: WUE is litres of cooling water per kWh of computing. Companies report between about 0.1 and 0.5 L/kWh, but each defines it a little differently.
questions.answer: Water usage effectiveness (WUE) divides the water used for cooling and humidity control by the electricity used by the IT equipment. Amazon reports 0.12 L/kWh for 2025, down from 0.25 in 2021, and puts the industry average at 0.84. Microsoft reports 0.30 L/kWh for its 2024 fiscal year, down from 0.49 in 2021, but its figure is based on withdrawal. Google does not headline a fleet WUE. All of these are self-reported. None includes the water used at power plants, which is often larger than the on-site figure.

questions.q: Are data centres pushing up electricity bills in the PJM region (Maryland, Pennsylvania, Ohio, New Jersey, Virginia, DC)?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Maryland's consumer advocate (Office of People's Counsel) puts out public bulletins on every PJM capacity auction because customers keep asking why bills rose, and it says residential customers 'should not be paying for these costs': https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MDOPC/bulletins/4006939 . questions.audience: Households in the 13 PJM states and DC
questions.verdict: Partly yes: PJM's independent market monitor estimates data-centre demand has added tens of billions of dollars to wholesale capacity costs, and those costs reach household bills.
questions.answer: PJM runs the grid across 13 US states and DC. Its independent market monitor estimates (these are estimates, not measured bills) that existing and forecast data-centre load raised capacity-market revenues by $7.3 billion (82%) in one auction, by $23.1 billion over three auctions, and by $29.4 billion over the last four. Through July 2026 it put data-centre load at 9% of the wholesale power price, or $10.48/MWh. These are wholesale costs. Utilities pass them on to retail customers over time, so the exact amount on any one household's bill depends on the utility and the state. Transmission costs tied to data centres are counted separately, on top of this.

questions.q: How long is the queue to connect new power plants to the US grid, and how many get built?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Queued Up is LBNL's annual report on this, and it is widely covered. APPA summary: https://www.publicpower.org/node/29114. The queue is a common reason given for why data centres cannot get power quickly.
questions.audience: Students and adults wondering why the grid can't just add supply for data centres
questions.verdict: Huge and slow: about 2,300 GW is waiting, a typical project now takes over four years, and most never get built.
questions.answer: At the end of 2024, US interconnection queues held about 1,400 GW of generation and about 890 GW of storage. That is far more than the country's whole power fleet, but most of it is proposals, not plants. The queue shrank about 12% from the year before, as withdrawals outpaced new requests. The median time from request to commercial operation has doubled, from under 2 years for plants built in 2000-2007 to over 4 years for those built in 2018-2024. Only 13% of capacity that applied between 2000 and 2019 was operating by the end of 2024, and 77% had withdrawn. These are measured counts from grid operators' queue data. Requests to connect large electricity users such as data centres are tracked separately.

questions.q: Are utilities' data-centre demand forecasts inflated by speculative requests?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Ohio industrial customers formally accused AEP of inflating its data-centre forecast, as described in a Harvard Salata Institute interview: https://salatainstitute.harvard.edu/?p=22020

questions.verdict: Some are. When AEP Ohio made data centres commit financially, its projected data-centre demand fell by more than half.
questions.answer: Developers often ask several utilities for power for the same project, so request totals can overstate what will actually be built. If the forecast load never arrives, customers may still have paid for capacity and wires.

questions.q: Should data centres pay for the regional transmission lines built because of them, not everyone in the region?
questions.evidence_people_ask: About 80 Maryland state lawmakers backed a FERC complaint on exactly this question in June 2026: https://www.utilitydive.com/news/lummis-power-up-act-ferc-large-load-interconnection/823244/
questions.audience: Maryland and other PJM residents far from the data-centre hubs
questions.verdict: This is being contested at the federal regulator (FERC). Under the current rules, costs are spread across the whole region.
questions.answer: PJM spreads half of certain regional transmission costs across its whole footprint, in proportion to each zone's load. It asked FERC to make PJM charge those projects to the zones where the data centres are. About 80 Maryland lawmakers backed the complaint, citing more than 80,000 MW of expected data-centre growth over 20 years. Both figures come from parties in the case, not from a neutral body.

questions.answer: PJM's independent market monitor compared the auctions as they actually cleared with what they would have cost without forecast data-centre load.
