questions.q: Have data centres caused a blackout in Virginia?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A widely shared industry headline asked whether Virginia 'narrowly avoided power cuts when 60 data centers dropped off the grid at once' (DCD, https://datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/virginia-narrowly-avoided-power-cuts-when-60-data-centers-dropped-off-the-grid-at-once). The US grid reliability body NERC also published an incident review, https://nerc.com/pa/rrm/ea/Documents/Incident_Review_Large_Load_Loss.pdf. Search budget ran out before I could collect Reddit or forum threads.
questions.audience: Northern Virginia residents, anyone who saw 'data centres nearly blacked out Virginia' headlines
questions.verdict: No: there has been no blackout so far. But data centres have suddenly dropped off the grid in large blocks, and grid operators treat that as a new risk.
questions.answer: In these events the data centres did not black anyone out. They disconnected themselves. On 10 July 2024 a lightning arrestor failed on a 230 kV line in northern Virginia, and about 1,500 MW of data-centre load switched to backup power. Utility equipment disconnected none of it. About 1,260 MW stayed off for hours. A similar 1,500 MW event followed on 17 February 2025. On 22 July 2026, about 3.8 GW moved from the grid to on-site generation, the largest such event PJM has recorded. None of the sources I read reports homes losing power. The risk is the grid suddenly losing that much demand, not running short of supply.

questions.q: Why is it a problem for the grid if data centres suddenly switch off?
questions.evidence_people_ask: This is the obvious follow-up to the Virginia headlines (if demand drops, isn't that good?). Grid operators discuss it openly: PJM's Operating Committee chair said data centres are 'disconnecting too early' (https://www.publicpower.org/periodical/article/pjm-dominion-review-large-load-transfer-event). NERC issued a Level 3 alert. A Utility Dive opinion piece is titled 'Data centers can vanish from the grid in seconds' (https://www.utilitydive.com/news/data-centers-vanish-grid-seconds-reliability-rules/827035/).
questions.audience: Curious adults and students learning how grids balance supply and demand
questions.verdict: A grid has to match supply and demand every second. Losing gigawatts of demand at once is as much of a shock as losing a big power plant.
questions.answer: Generators are tuned to the demand they expect. If a big block of demand vanishes, frequency and voltage rise until operators cut generation. On 22 July 2026, PJM's total load fell from 99,984 MW to 96,205 MW, about 3.8%. Operators brought the imbalance back within limits in nine minutes, against a 30-minute NERC standard. Operators say data-centre equipment is too sensitive to voltage dips and disconnects too early. NERC issued a Level 3 'essential actions' alert on 4 May 2026. Minimum 'ride-through' requirements for computing loads are expected in NERC standards in 2027. That is a forecast, not yet a rule.

questions.q: Can Texas switch off data centres during a power emergency?
questions.evidence_people_ask: After Uri, Texans ask whether big new loads will be cut before homes. Texas legislators answered with Senate Bill 6 (2025), https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm.
questions.audience: Texas households, students studying energy policy
questions.verdict: Yes. Under Texas law (SB 6), new large loads of 75 MW or more must be able to be cut off during rolling outages, and ERCOT can order them onto backup generators.
questions.answer: Texas Senate Bill 6 sets a 75 MW threshold for 'large load' customers, which covers most big data centres. Before connecting, these customers must agree a protocol, including equipment, so their load can be curtailed during 'firm load shed' (rolling outages). Ahead of or during an energy emergency, ERCOT can tell the utility to make the customer either run its on-site backup generators or cut its load. ERCOT must also buy demand reductions from large loads, with at least 24 hours' notice. This is law, not a measured outcome. How often these powers have been used is not in the sources I read.

questions.answer: Some AI work, such as training, can be paused or shifted, unlike a hospital or a home freezer. Google says it reduced the power used by machine-learning work during three grid events with Omaha Public Power District. questions.verdict: About 6.7 TWh a year, roughly 1.4% of what the world's data centres used in 2025.
questions.answer: US nuclear plants ran at about 91% of their maximum output in 2025 (EIA). At that rate, an 835 MW reactor makes about 835 MW × 8,760 hours × 0.91 ≈ 6.7 TWh of electricity a year. That is generation, measured at the plant. The IEA estimates world data-centre consumption at 485 TWh in 2025. One restarted reactor would equal about 1.4% of that. This is Hum's own estimate. It assumes Crane runs like an average US reactor, which it has not yet shown.

figures.quote: add approximately 835 megawatts of carbon-free energy to the grid

questions.q: Is nuclear power actually low-carbon?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A perennial question whenever tech companies call nuclear 'carbon-free' (e.g. Constellation/Microsoft release). https://world-nuclear.org/information-library/energy-and-the-environment/carbon-dioxide-emissions-from-electricity
questions.verdict: Yes, over its life cycle. Reviews put it at roughly 5–12 g CO2e per kWh, similar to wind.
questions.answer: A nuclear plant emits almost no CO2 while running. Mining, fuel making, construction and decommissioning do add emissions. Across peer-reviewed studies the IPCC's median for the whole life cycle is 12 g CO2-equivalent per kWh, similar to wind. A UNECE assessment found 5.1–6.4 g. Ember puts the average for the world's grid at 473 g/kWh. So 'carbon-free' is a simplification, but nuclear is among the lowest-carbon sources. These figures are quoted here through the World Nuclear Association, an industry body, so check them against the originals.

questions.verdict: Demand for big turbines outran factory output, so new orders wait years.
questions.answer: GE Vernova, one of the biggest makers, reported gas equipment backlog plus reserved production slots of 116 GW in mid-2026, up from 100 GW a quarter earlier. It expects at least 125 GW under contract by year-end. Its factories plan to produce 20 GW of turbines a year from late 2026, with targets of 24 GW in 2028 and 30 GW in 2030 (company claims). At 20 GW a year, 116 GW is about 5.8 years of output. That is a rough calculation, because output is rising and not every reservation becomes an order. The IEA says turbine deliveries now face lead times of several years. Some reported waits run to 2031, but I could not confirm that against a primary source.

questions.q: Is a data centre running on gas cleaner or dirtier than one on the normal grid?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A common question under news about gas-powered AI campuses (e.g. coverage of GE Vernova backlogs and the Meta/Entergy gas plants). Specific forum threads were not checked because the search budget ran out.
questions.verdict: Gas is about half as carbon-intensive as coal, but a bit more than the average US grid mix.
questions.answer: Counting only CO2 from burning fuel at the plant, the EIA reports that US gas generation emitted 0.96 lb of CO2 per kWh in 2023, about 435 g. Coal emitted 2.31 lb (about 1,048 g), and the whole US grid averaged about 0.81 lb (about 367 g), because it includes nuclear, wind, hydro and solar. So supplying a data centre with new gas instead of the average US mix adds roughly 18% more CO2 per kWh it consumes. Replacing coal would roughly halve it. These are fleet averages. A new efficient plant does better and a simple turbine does worse. Methane leaking upstream is not included.

figures.quote: Natural gas: 0.96
figures.check_note: No literal 'Natural gas: 0.96' text on the page. The 2023 table row reads 'Natural gas | 1,806,063 | 790 | 871 | 0.96' in the pounds-per-kWh column, so the value matches. 0.96 x 453.6 = 435 g/kWh is correct.

figures.quote: Coal: 2.31
figures.check_note: Table row 'Coal | 675,115 | 709 | 781 | 2.31' (lb/kWh, 2023), not literal 'Coal: 2.31' text. The value matches; 2.31 x 453.6 = 1,048 g/kWh is correct.

figures.quote: about 0.81 pounds of CO2 emissions per kWh
figures.check_note: Page text: 'which is about 0.81 pounds of CO 2 emissions per kWh' (subscript spacing only). The table's all-sources row also gives 0.81; 367 g/kWh is correct.

figures.claim: Gas vs US average: 0.96 / 0.81 = 1.185, so about 18% more CO2 per kWh
figures.quote: about 0.81 pounds of CO2 emissions per kWh
figures.check_note: The quote for 0.81 is verified. Derived ratio: 0.96/0.81 = 1.185, which rounds to 1.19, not 1.18 (1.18 is truncated). About 18% more CO2 is still fair.

gaps: Upstream methane leakage and life-cycle emissions of gas are not included; I did not fetch a primary source for them.
There is no per-plant emissions data for specific data-centre gas plants.
The EIA FAQ figures are for 2023; I did not check whether a 2024 or 2025 update exists.

questions.q: What is the difference between a gas 'peaker' turbine and a combined-cycle plant, and why does it matter for data centres?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Comes up often around on-site turbines at AI campuses (e.g. xAI Memphis) and utility combined-cycle plans such as Entergy's for Meta. Specific forum URLs were not gathered because the search budget ran out.
questions.verdict: Combined-cycle plants reuse waste heat and burn about a third less gas per kWh than simple turbines.
questions.answer: A simple gas turbine (often a 'peaker') burns gas and loses the hot exhaust. A combined-cycle plant uses that exhaust heat to drive a second, steam turbine. The EIA's 2024 tested heat rates show 7,548 Btu of gas per kWh for US combined-cycle plants and 10,999 Btu for gas turbines. That works out to about 45% versus 31% efficiency, and about 46% more fuel, and so more CO2, per kWh from a simple turbine. Quick, on-site setups for data centres often use smaller turbines or engines, which tend to be less efficient. Grid-scale plants built for big campuses are usually combined-cycle.

questions.q: How much extra CO2 could the new gas power for US data centres add?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A recurring reader question under coverage of EIA's gas build-out and the IEA's Energy and AI report (e.g. https://www.mychesco.com/a/news/pennsylvania/data-centers-drive-4-4-gigawatt-pa-gas-power-buildout/).
questions.verdict: Very roughly 55-60 million tonnes of CO2 a year by 2030, if the IEA's forecast holds.
questions.answer: The IEA forecasts gas adding over 130 TWh a year of US generation for data centres by 2030. At the 2023 US gas average of 0.96 lb of CO2 per kWh (about 0.435 kg), that works out to roughly 57 million tonnes of CO2 a year. This is my own calculation from a forecast and a fleet average, not a published estimate. For scale, the IEA puts CO2 from electricity used by all the world's data centres at 180 million tonnes today. Newer combined-cycle plants would come in lower, and turbines or methane leaks would push it higher.

figures.check_note: Same IEA quote as qi0 fi2, verified on the page; 'over 130 TWh'.

figures.claim: 130e9 kWh x 0.96 lb x 0.4536 kg/lb = about 56.6 Mt CO2 per year (lower bound, since the IEA says 'over 130 TWh')
figures.quote: Natural gas: 0.96
figures.check_note: 0.96 lb/kWh is verified in the EIA table (table form, not literal 'Natural gas: 0.96'). 130e9 x 0.96 x 0.4536 = 56.6 Mt, which rounds to 57. Correct, and it is a lower bound.

questions.q: Do official statistics count the gas plants that data centres build for themselves?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Asked whenever on-site AI turbines are in the news (xAI Memphis, West Texas 'private grid' projects). See MyChesCo's note that EIA totals exclude on-site plants: https://www.mychesco.com/a/news/pennsylvania/data-centers-drive-4-4-gigawatt-pa-gas-power-buildout/
questions.audience: Adults and journalists trying to size the gas build-out
questions.verdict: Often not: the EIA planned-capacity totals cover grid-connected plants, so on-site gas is undercounted.
questions.answer: The EIA data behind the 60.4 GW planned-gas figure covers generators planned for connection to local or regional grids. They do not include gas plants that data-centre operators may build on-site for their own use. Off-grid projects can be large. One West Texas project, GW Ranch, received an air permit for up to 7.7 GW of gas-turbine generation for a private grid supporting data centres. That is a permit ceiling, not a built plant. No public count of all on-site gas capacity at data centres was found. National totals are therefore a floor, not the full picture.

questions.answer: Louisiana's Public Service Commission approved Entergy Louisiana's plan in August 2025. questions.q: Is most new US power capacity gas because of AI?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Frequently asked alongside EIA's record 2026 capacity-addition outlook (Industrial Info: https://www.industrialinfo.com/news/article/eia-sees-us-hitting-record-grid-capacity-additions-in-2026-adding-86-gw--354083) and think-tank pieces on gas and AI (https://americanactionforum.org/insight/ai-data-center-power-surge-shifting-trends-toward-natural-gas).
questions.verdict: No: in 2026 most planned additions are solar and batteries, but gas's share of plans is climbing.
questions.answer: For 2026, developers told the EIA they plan 6.3 GW of new US gas capacity: 3.3 GW combined-cycle and 2.8 GW combustion turbines. That is a small slice of a record year dominated by solar and batteries. Gas's share of planned capacity rose from 11.1% in 2024 to 18.1% in 2026. Larger gas additions are planned for later in the decade, partly driven by data centres. The EIA says that if data-centre demand grows faster than expected, the extra generation would mainly come from running existing gas plants harder. Plans can slip or be cancelled.

questions.q: Are coal plants really being kept open because of AI data centres?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Widely covered reader-facing investigations framing exactly this question, e.g. DeSmog 'These 15 Coal Plants Would Have Retired. Then Came AI and Trump' (Dec 2025), republished by Naked Capitalism and others: https://www.desmog.com/2025/12/12/15-coal-plant-retirements-delayed-ai-data-centers-trump-doe-orders/ ; Frontier Group 'Data center energy use is giving old, dirty power plants a new lease on life': https://frontiergroup.org/?p=5705. (Web search budget ran out before Reddit/forum threads could be checked.)
questions.verdict: Partly. Data centres are one main reason utilities give, but federal emergency orders and gas prices also play big roles.
questions.answer: In 2025 US operators planned to retire 8.5 GW of coal capacity but only 2.6 GW actually closed (EIA, measured). 4.8 GW was pushed to a later year and 1.1 GW of closures were cancelled. Some of those delays came from Department of Energy emergency orders, not from a utility's own choice. Where utilities chose to delay, several point to data-centre demand: Southern Company, for example, cites data centres in legal documents. The IEA puts the overall US slowdown down to policy support and higher gas prices. So data centres are a real reason, but not the only one. EIA does not say why each delay happened.

questions.q: Which power companies have delayed closing coal plants, and until when?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Local and national coverage lists the utilities by name, a frequent question in utility-customer and state news: https://www.desmog.com/2025/12/12/15-coal-plant-retirements-delayed-ai-data-centers-trump-doe-orders/ ; Power Engineering 'Coal plant retirements: a slowdown and will it matter?': https://www.power-eng.com/coal/coal-plant-retirements-a-slowdown-and-will-it-matter/
questions.verdict: Several large US utilities have pushed coal closures back by years, some into the late 2030s or 2040s.
questions.answer: These are company plans, reported by journalists, and they can change. Southern Company pushed back retirement of units at Plants Bowen and Scherer in Georgia to as late as 1 January 2039. Dominion Energy no longer expects to retire any of its coal plants until at least 2045. Its 2023 plan projected that data-centre demand would nearly quadruple by 2038. Alliant Energy moved Wisconsin's Columbia Energy Center closure from 2026 to 2029. Omaha's North Omaha Unit 5 was moved from 2023 to 2026, citing data-centre demand. A 2025 count found 22 delayed coal units, about 12 GW, or 21% of the coal then planned to retire or convert.

questions.q: What is a DOE emergency order, and who pays to keep these coal plants running?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The orders, starting with Michigan's J.H. Campbell plant, prompted widespread customer coverage and questions about costs: https://www.desmog.com/2025/12/12/15-coal-plant-retirements-delayed-ai-data-centers-trump-doe-orders/ ; Industrial Info: https://www.industrialinfo.com/iirenergy/industry-news/article/us-coal-fired-power-plant-retirements-slowed-in-2025-future-is-uncertain--357093
questions.verdict: The US Energy Department used an emergency power-law clause to order plants to stay available, and the costs fall on electricity customers.
questions.answer: Under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act, the Department of Energy can order a plant to stay available to run for grid reliability. In 2025 it used this power on several coal plants. Industrial Info estimates these orders kept about 3,240 MW of coal from retiring on schedule. Michigan's J.H. Campbell plant was costing more than $615,000 a day as of September 2025. Closing it had been projected to save customers more than $650 million by 2050. That cost figure comes from the plant's owner, as reported by journalists. In another order, DOE pointed to 15 GW of data-centre load growth in the PJM region.

questions.q: Do data centres run on coal power?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Common question when people learn coal plants are staying open; IEA addresses it directly in its Energy and AI report: https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai/energy-supply-for-ai ; frames in coverage like https://frontiergroup.org/?p=5705
questions.verdict: Partly. Coal is the biggest single source of data-centre electricity worldwide, about 30%, but this varies a lot by country.
questions.answer: Data centres draw from the grid, so their electricity mix follows the local grid. The IEA estimates that coal supplies about 30% of data-centre electricity worldwide, the largest single source. In China it is nearly 70%. questions.q: If Google says it runs on 100% renewable energy, why does it also say it is only about 65% carbon-free?
questions.evidence_people_ask: I used up the web-search budget before I could pull a Reddit or forum thread. Interest in this question shows in trade press asking what Google's environmental report says about energy (https://energydigital.com/news/what-googles-environment-report-says-about-energy) and in Electricity Maps explaining Google's hourly reporting (https://www.electricitymaps.com/content/google-reporting). A real reader question still needs to be found.
questions.audience: Everyday adults who see '100% renewable' claims in tech marketing
questions.verdict: Both are true because they measure different things: 100% is an annual total, and 65% is hour by hour on the local grid.
questions.answer: Google buys as much renewable electricity each year as it uses worldwide. It has done this for nine years in a row, and it calls this 'global and annual' matching. That does not mean clean power reached its data centres in every hour. Night, calm weather and grids heavy in coal or gas all leave gaps. When Google instead counts each hour on each local grid, its data centres and offices reached about 65% carbon-free energy (CFE) in 2025, roughly flat from 66% in 2024, while its electricity use grew 37%. These are Google's own figures, checked by a third party under limited assurance. They are not independent measurements.

questions.q: Does matching every hour actually cut more emissions than buying enough renewables over a year, and what does it cost?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The GHG Protocol Scope 2 consultation, which received nearly 1,100 responses from 56 countries, centred on this trade-off, and the respondents split on whether hourly matching improves integrity (https://ghgprotocol.org/ghg-protocol-public-consultations). Google cites research on this point in its 2026 report.
questions.verdict: Models say yes once the hourly match passes about 85%, and the cost rises steeply near 100%.
questions.answer: One peer-reviewed-style modelling study (Riepin and Brown, TU Berlin) compared the two approaches for European grids. Both cut system emissions. Hourly '24/7' matching cut more once the target passed about 85%. In one 2030 case it cut local emissions by up to 0.4 MtCO2 a year, against 0.2 Mt for annual matching. A 90-95% hourly match cost only a little more than annual matching. A 98% match cost 54% more. A 100% match cost 42% more with long-duration storage, or 15% more with advanced clean firm technologies. These are model estimates, not measurements.

questions.q: Will companies be required to match their clean energy hour by hour?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The GHG Protocol's public consultation on Scope 2 (20 October 2025 to 31 January 2026) received nearly 1,100 responses from 56 countries (https://ghgprotocol.org/ghg-protocol-public-consultations).
questions.verdict: It has been proposed but not decided. Most respondents, especially companies, did not support the draft as written.
questions.answer: The GHG Protocol is the main global rulebook for corporate carbon accounting. It has proposed that companies using certificates match them to their consumption hour by hour, and from grid regions that can actually deliver the power. Smaller users could be exempt. Its consultation ran from October 2025 to January 2026 and drew nearly 1,100 responses. Support for hourly matching and deliverability as proposed was low, especially among companies and industry groups. Reporting programmes and data providers were more positive. A revised standard is expected in late 2027 at the earliest, phased in over several years. Nothing is final.

questions.q: How fast is a big AI company's own electricity use growing?
questions.evidence_people_ask: I have no direct forum evidence because the search budget ran out. News coverage of Google's environmental reports, for example Energy Digital (https://energydigital.com/news/what-googles-environment-report-says-about-energy), focuses on rising energy use.
questions.verdict: Google's electricity use grew 37% in one year, to about 43.6 TWh in 2025, and 97% of it went to data centres.
questions.answer: Google reports that its total electricity consumption rose from 31.7 TWh in 2024 to 43.6 TWh in 2025. Its data centres used 42.4 TWh of that. Consumption has more than doubled since 2021 (18.1 TWh). For scale, the IEA estimates world data-centre consumption at about 485 TWh in 2025, so Google's data centres would be roughly 9% of it, though the two figures are counted differently. This rapid growth is why holding hourly clean-energy shares steady is hard: new clean supply must grow as fast as demand.

questions.verdict: A REC is a tradable claim to 1 MWh of renewable generation somewhere on the grid; it does not change which electrons reach you.
questions.answer: In the US, a REC is created each time a renewable plant generates one megawatt-hour and puts it on the grid. In Europe the same idea is called a Guarantee of Origin. The certificate is separated from the physical power and can be sold on its own. The US EPA explains why certificates exist: grid electricity says nothing about where it came from, so certificates are how a 'renewable' claim is tracked. So buying one gives you the legal right to claim that megawatt-hour, but the data centre is still drawing whatever mix the local grid supplies at that moment. Whether the purchase also causes new clean power to be built depends on the type of deal.

questions.q: Do renewable energy certificates actually cut emissions?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Nature Climate Change study and the ScienceDaily write-up were both posted and discussed on Hacker News: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=31694802 and https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=31746014
questions.verdict: Often much less than the paperwork suggests: a peer-reviewed study found certificates inflated companies' reported cuts.
questions.answer: A 2022 peer-reviewed study in Nature Climate Change looked at 115 companies with science-based climate targets. Between 2015 and 2019 they reported a 31% fall in emissions, but without counting purchased certificates the drop was about 10%. The authors conclude that widespread REC use has led to an inflated estimate of mitigation, and that if the trend continues, 42% of promised Scope 2 cuts would not happen in the real world. The core problem: a cheap certificate from an existing wind farm usually does not cause any new clean generation. Long-term contracts that pay for new plants are a different case. This is an estimate from a sample of companies, not a measurement of the whole market.

Its location-based figure, based on the actual grids, kept rising steadily: from 4.3 million tonnes in 2020 to 12.0 million in 2025, as electricity use more than tripled to about 37 TWh. The jump is explained in Microsoft's own report: in February 2025 it stopped buying 'spot' unbundled certificates and no longer counts them. So the dramatic change is in the paperwork; the grid-based figure shows the underlying growth. These are company-reported, assured figures.

questions.q: Meta says its data centres had almost zero emissions from electricity. How is that possible?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Recurring HN skepticism about '100% renewable' tech claims backed by certificates, e.g. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=24095807 and https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=13132856 ; Guardian investigation of tech data-centre emissions https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/sep/15/data-center-gas-emissions-tech

questions.verdict: Because Meta reports the market-based figure after matching 100% of its electricity with renewable purchases; on the grids it actually uses, the figure was about 5.9 million tonnes.
questions.answer: In its 2025 data index, Meta reports 2024 market-based Scope 2 emissions for its data centres of 135 tonnes CO2e. The location-based figure for the same data centres, using the grids they sit on, is 5,862,614 tonnes, about 43,000 times larger. Those data centres used about 18.1 TWh of electricity, and Meta says more than 99% came from the grid while 100% was 'matched' with renewable energy. Both numbers are company-reported. The small one reflects contracts and certificates; the big one reflects what the local grids emitted, on average, to supply that power. Neither tells you exactly what extra emissions Meta caused.

questions.q: What does Amazon (or any tech company) mean when it says it matched 100% of its electricity with renewables?
questions.evidence_people_ask: HN thread on Google's 2017 '100% renewable' pledge asking whether off-site purchases mean running on clean power: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=13132856 ; HN comment 'They don't run 100% on renewable electricity' https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=24095807
questions.verdict: It is an annual total: renewable megawatt-hours bought or counted over a year equal the megawatt-hours used, not that clean power flowed every hour.
questions.answer: Amazon says 100% of the electricity it consumed in 2025 was matched with renewable sources, for the third year running. Its methodology explains the sum: renewable output from projects it backs, plus the renewable share of local grids, divided by its total use, counted from 1 January to 31 December. It retires certificates for each claimed megawatt-hour. It 'aims' to buy in the same grids but says that in some cases it buys elsewhere. So a data centre can run on gas at night while solar bought in the afternoon, or in another region, balances the yearly books. This is a company claim with third-party assurance, not an hour-by-hour measurement.

figures.quote: 100% of the electricity consumed by Amazon was matched with renewable energy sources in 2025, for the third consecutive year
figures.check_note: On the Amazon carbon-free-energy page. 100% matches.

figures.quote: Amazon’s renewable energy percentage is calculated on an annual basis, from January 1 through December 31 of each year, and is assured by an independent third-party assurance provider.
figures.check_note: Exact sentence in the Amazon methodology PDF.

figures.claim: Amazon aims to buy in the same grids but may buy elsewhere
figures.quote: Amazon aims to procure renewable electricity in the same grids where we consume electricity. In certain cases, we may procure renewable energy in other locations.
figures.check_note: Exact text in the Amazon methodology PDF.

figures.claim: Amazon: 700+ projects, 40+ GW capacity
figures.quote: 700+ carbon-free energy projects worldwide, with the capacity to generate 40+ gigawatts of electricity
figures.check_note: On the Amazon page. 40+ GW matches as low = 40.

gaps: Amazon does not publish an hourly matching percentage or separate data-centre (AWS) location-based emissions in the sources fetched.
Share of Amazon's matched MWh from out-of-region purchases is not disclosed.

questions.q: Is the CO2 figure for a Google Gemini prompt market-based? What would it be on the actual grid?
questions.evidence_people_ask: HN reader on Google's AI-prompt energy data asks: 'Does the market-based approach let Google claim lower emissions?' https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44982714
questions.audience: AI users, students, journalists covering AI energy
questions.verdict: Yes, Google's 0.03 g per prompt uses a market-based factor; on Google's grid-average (location-based) factor it would be roughly three to four times higher.
questions.answer: Google estimates the median Gemini text prompt uses 0.24 Wh and emits 0.03 g CO2e. Its technical paper says all emissions figures are market-based. For 2024, Google's location-based factor was 345 g per kWh; clean-energy purchases reduced that by 251 g, leaving a net market-based factor of 94 g per kWh. Applying the grid-average 345 g/kWh to 0.24 Wh gives about 0.08 g per prompt, versus about 0.02 g on 94 g/kWh (Google's 0.03 g also includes other parts of the footprint). Either way it is tiny per prompt; the point is which accounting is used. These are Google's own estimates for May 2025, not independent measurements.

figures.claim: Median Gemini text prompt: 0.24 Wh and 0.03 gCO2e
figures.quote: we estimate the median Gemini Apps text prompt uses 0.24 watt-hours (Wh) of energy, emits 0.03 grams of carbon dioxide equivalent (gCO2e)
figures.check_note: On the Google Cloud blog. 0.24 Wh and 0.03 gCO2e match.

figures.claim: Paper uses market-based emissions for all metrics
figures.quote: We consider MB GHG emissions for all metrics presented in this paper.
figures.check_note: Exact sentence in the arXiv 2508.15734 HTML.

figures.quote: Google’s LB emission factor was 345 gCO2e/kWh
figures.check_note: On the arXiv page. 345 matches.

figures.claim: Google 2024 net market-based emission factor 94 gCO2e/kWh
figures.quote: the net MB emission factor was 94 gCO2e/kWh
figures.check_note: On the arXiv page. 94 matches.

figures.claim: Location-based per-prompt operational CO2: 0.24 Wh x 345 g/kWh = 0.083 g; market-based 0.24 x 94 = 0.023 g
figures.quote: Google’s LB emission factor was 345 gCO2e/kWh
figures.check_note: The 345 g/kWh quote is present. The figures are derived arithmetic: 0.24 x 0.345 = 0.0828 (about 0.083) and 0.24 x 0.094 = 0.0226 (about 0.023). Both are correct as derived values.

gaps: Google's reported 0.03 g includes components beyond operational electricity (e.g. embodied hardware); the exact split was not verified, so the 0.08 g figure covers electricity only.

questions.q: What is 24/7 carbon-free energy, and how clean is the cloud region my app runs in?
questions.evidence_people_ask: HN discussion of whether off-site renewable purchases equal running on clean power given that wind and solar vary: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=13132856 ; HN thread on hour-by-hour Matched Clean Power Index (23 comments) https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45789640
questions.verdict: It means checking clean supply hour by hour in the same place; by that test Google's regions range from about 20% clean (Mumbai) to 100% (Stockholm).
questions.answer: Annual matching just balances a year's totals. 24/7 carbon-free energy asks a harder question: in each hour, in that location, how much of the power used was carbon-free? Google publishes this per cloud region. For 2025 it reports Northern Virginia, the world's biggest data-centre hub, at 57% carbon-free with a grid intensity of 343 g CO2e/kWh; Iowa at 88%; Mumbai at 20% (598 g/kWh); and Stockholm at 100% (19 g/kWh). Google describes the figure as the average share of time your workload runs on carbon-free energy. These are Google's own calculations, including its contracts in each region.

questions.q: Are the rules changing so companies must match clean power hour by hour?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The GHG Protocol's Scope 2 consultation drew nearly 1,100 responses from 56 countries (https://ghgprotocol.org/sites/default/files/2026-07/S2-ExecutiveSummary-PublicConsultation%20ummaryofFeedback-2026.07.29.pdf); HN thread on hourly matching index https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45789640
questions.audience: Journalists, policy students, sustainability staff, general adults following tech climate claims
questions.verdict: Proposed but not decided: hourly matching got low support in consultation, and the standard-setter has asked for more work on several options.
questions.answer: The GHG Protocol, whose rules nearly all company carbon reports follow, proposed that large organisations match certificates to consumption hourly and from grid regions the power could plausibly reach; smaller ones would be exempt. The consultation ran from 20 October 2025 to 31 January 2026 and received nearly 1,100 responses. Its July 2026 summary reports low support for hourly matching and deliverability as proposed, especially among companies. The board then asked for further work on several market-based approaches. Earlier, the Protocol expected a revised standard in late 2027, phased in over years. So as of October 2026, annual matching is still allowed.

questions.q: My electricity supplier says my tariff is '100% renewable'. Is that the same trick?
questions.evidence_people_ask: HN discussion of Matched's Clean Power Index comparing UK suppliers' hourly renewable match (23 comments) https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45789640

questions.answer: Household green tariffs usually rely on the same certificates as tech companies (Guarantees of Origin in the UK and Europe), matched over a year. Matched, a UK company that compares supplier contracts with demand hour by hour using public data, says it has seen electricity branded as 100% renewable that is actually only 55% on an hourly basis. These are one company's estimates, not an official measurement, but they show the same gap as data centres: annual totals look cleaner than what happens hour by hour.

questions.q: How much CO2 does it take to make one Nvidia H100 AI chip?
questions.evidence_people_ask: I could not search forums because this run had used up its shared search budget, so there is no Reddit or forum link here. Supporting evidence: Nvidia published product carbon footprint summaries in FY26 because customers ask for these numbers. Its FY26 report says it answers customer CDP and EcoVadis requests: https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/documents/NVIDIA-Sustainability-Report-Fiscal-Year-2026.pdf
questions.audience: Everyday adults and students curious about the 'hidden' carbon in AI hardware
questions.verdict: About 1.3 tonnes of CO2e for a board of eight H100 GPUs, or roughly 164 kg per GPU. This is Nvidia's own estimate, reviewed by a third party.
questions.answer: Nvidia's product carbon footprint is a company claim, done by WSP and reviewed by a third party. It puts the cradle-to-gate footprint of one HGX H100 baseboard at 1,312 kg CO2e. Cradle-to-gate means everything from mining the materials to the board leaving the factory. The board holds eight H100 GPUs plus memory, networking chips and cooling hardware. Divided by eight, that is about 164 kg per GPU. Nvidia did not publish that per-chip figure; it is our arithmetic. The biggest shares are the high-bandwidth memory (42%), the chips (25%) and the cooling parts (18%). The figure leaves out the rest of the server, the data-centre building, running the board and disposing of it.

figures.claim: Cradle-to-gate carbon footprint of one Nvidia HGX H100 baseboard (8 GPUs)
figures.quote: Our PCF determined that the carbon footprint from cradle-to-gate for one HGX H100 GPU baseboard is 1,312 kg CO2e.
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim in the H100 PCF PDF; 1,312 kg CO2e matches mid.

figures.claim: Per-GPU share: 1,312 kg / 8 GPUs = about 164 kg CO2e per GPU slot (our arithmetic; it includes a share of the board's memory, cooling and networking)
figures.quote: It features eight H100 GPUs, each with 80GB of HBM3 memory, and utilizes NVLink and NVSwitch for high-speed interconnects.
figures.check_note: Quote on page (eight H100 GPUs, 80GB HBM3). 1312/8 = 164 is correct arithmetic, labelled as derived.

figures.claim: Share of H100 board footprint from high-bandwidth memory (42%), with ICs 25% and thermal parts 18%
figures.quote: The production of high bandwidth memory (42%), integrated circuits (25%) and thermal components (18%) are significant drivers of the carbon footprint.
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; HBM 42%, ICs 25%, thermal 18% match.

gaps: Nvidia publishes no footprint for a single H100 GPU, only for the 8-GPU board.
The footprint of the full server (CPUs, storage, chassis) and of building the data centre is not included.
End-of-life (disposal and recycling) emissions are excluded by design.
questions.angle: chips: manufacturing energy, water and emissions (TSMC, Nvidia GPUs), embodied carbon

questions.q: Is making AI chips worse for the climate than running them?
questions.evidence_people_ask: I could not gather forum evidence because the run's search budget was spent. Google's own lifecycle paper exists to answer this question, which suggests the question comes up. 'Embodied vs operational' is also a common question in AI-sustainability discussions: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.01671
questions.audience: Adults weighing whether hardware or electricity matters more
questions.verdict: No. Over its life, AI hardware usually emits much more from the electricity it uses than from being made, unless it runs on very clean power.
questions.answer: Google authors studied five generations of their TPU AI chips across the whole hardware life. Their paper is published on arXiv; we did not confirm whether it has been peer reviewed. It found running the chips (operational emissions) makes up 70% to 90% of lifetime emissions, and manufacturing under 25%. A rough check with Nvidia's numbers points the same way. An HGX H100 board's typical power draw is 5,600 W. Run all year, that is about 49,000 kWh, or roughly 23 tonnes of CO2 at the world-average grid (Ember, 473 g/kWh). Making the board took about 1.3 tonnes. On a very clean grid, manufacturing becomes a bigger share. All of these are estimates, not measurements from a particular data centre.

figures.claim: Operational share of AI system lifetime emissions: about 70% (market-based, counting Google's clean-power purchases) to about 90% (location-based)
figures.quote: Operational emissions are ∼70% of emissions when including Google's CFE procurement
figures.check_note: On the arXiv HTML page (the ~ is MathML). The full sentence goes on to say ~90% when not counting CFE (location-based), which supports low 70 / high 90.

figures.claim: Rule of thumb without counting clean-power purchases: embodied about 10%, operational about 90%
figures.quote: embodied emissions are ∼10% and operational emissions are ∼90% of an AI system's lifetime emissions.
figures.check_note: The rule-of-thumb sentence is on the page: embodied ~10%, operational ~90%. Matches mid 10.

figures.claim: One year of operation of an HGX H100 board: 5.6 kW x 8,760 h = about 49,056 kWh. At Hum's held Ember world-average grid intensity of 473 g/kWh, that is about 23.2 t CO2 per year, compared with 1.312 t to manufacture it (our arithmetic; it assumes the board runs at typical power all year and leaves out cooling overhead)
figures.quote: Typical power consumption 5600 W
figures.check_note: The PDF datasheet shows 'Typical power consumption' and '5600 W' as table cells on separate lines, not as one sentence. 5.6 kW x 8760 h = 49,056 kWh is correct (derived).

gaps: Real utilisation and data-centre overhead (PUE) for H100 deployments are not published, so the 49,000 kWh per year is an upper-bound style illustration.
Hardware service life (3, 5 or 6 years) changes the split, and it is not standardised.
Comparable lifecycle studies for Nvidia GPUs that include the use phase were not found.
questions.angle: chips: manufacturing energy, water and emissions (TSMC, Nvidia GPUs), embodied carbon

questions.q: Why does Nvidia's newer B200 have a bigger manufacturing footprint than the H100?
questions.evidence_people_ask: No forum links, because the search budget was exhausted. Nvidia raises the comparison itself in its FY26 sustainability report, claiming a 24% cut per workload, which invites the question of why the absolute number rose: https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/documents/NVIDIA-Sustainability-Report-Fiscal-Year-2026.pdf
questions.audience: Tech-curious adults following new chip launches
questions.verdict: Mostly because of memory. The B200 board carries more than twice as much high-bandwidth memory, and memory is the largest slice of the footprint.
questions.answer: These are Nvidia's own footprints, each reviewed by a third party and measured from cradle to gate (materials through the factory door). One HGX B200 board comes to 2,274 kg CO2e, against 1,312 kg for an HGX H100 board. Memory is 49% of the B200 footprint, about 1,100 kg, compared with about 550 kg (42%) on the H100. Each B200 GPU carries 180 GB of HBM3E memory, against 80 GB of HBM3 on the H100. Nvidia says embodied carbon per unit of AI work fell 24% between the generations, because the B200 does much more work. That is a company claim, and its method sits in a blog we did not review.

figures.claim: Cradle-to-gate footprint of one HGX B200 baseboard (8 GPUs)
figures.quote: Our PCF determined that the carbon footprint from cradle-to-gate for one HGX B200 GPU baseboard is 2,274 kg CO2e.
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim in the B200 PCF PDF; 2,274 kg CO2e matches.

figures.claim: Memory share of B200 board footprint (49%), about 1,114 kg by our arithmetic (0.49 x 2,274); Nvidia's chart shows 1,123 kg
figures.quote: The production of high bandwidth memory (49%), integrated circuits (28%) and thermal components (12%) are significant drivers of the carbon footprint.
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; 49% matches. The chart value 1,123 also appears in the PDF.

figures.claim: Memory per B200 GPU
figures.quote: It features eight NVIDIA Blackwell B200 GPUs, each with 180 GB of HBM3E memory
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; 180 GB HBM3E matches.

figures.claim: Claimed reduction in embodied carbon per unit of large AI workload, B200 vs H100
figures.quote: A comparative analysis of these PCF summaries demonstrates a 24% reduction of embodied carbon emissions across large workloads such as AI training and inference between generations.
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim in the NVIDIA FY2026 Sustainability Report; 24% matches.

gaps: The method behind the 24% per-workload claim (in an Nvidia blog) was not read or checked independently.
No independent lifecycle study of Blackwell GPUs was found.
Footprints for Vera Rubin and later generations are not yet published.

questions.q: How much electricity does it take to make AI chips?
questions.evidence_people_ask: I could not gather forum evidence because the search budget was used up. Greenpeace East Asia's April 2025 report argues chipmaking energy is 'surprisingly overlooked', and the report was widely covered: https://www.greenpeace.org/eastasia/press/68006/artificial-intelligence-supply-chain-threatens-climate-progress-in-east-asia/
questions.audience: Adults who know data centres use a lot of power and wonder about the factories
questions.verdict: An estimated 1 TWh in 2024. That is small next to data centres' 415 TWh, but it is forecast to grow up to 170-fold by 2030.
questions.answer: Greenpeace East Asia and researcher Alex de Vries estimated the electricity used to make the main AI chips: Nvidia A100, H100, H200 and B100/B200, and AMD MI300X, including their logic and memory wafers. It rose from 218 GWh in 2023 to nearly 984 GWh in 2024. That is electricity consumed at factories, mostly in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan. It is about 0.24% of the 415 TWh the IEA counts for data centres in 2024. Their 2030 projection, based on McKinsey's forecasts of chip-wafer demand, is 11,550 to 37,238 GWh. These are bottom-up estimates from an advocacy group, because chipmakers do not report AI-specific figures. Google's TPUs and general server parts are not included.

figures.unit: GWh per year (2023 value in low, 2024 value in mid)
figures.quote: Global electricity consumption from AI chipmaking increased by more than 350% year on year, from 218 GWh in 2023 to nearly 984 GWh in 2024.
figures.publisher: Greenpeace East Asia (with Alex de Vries)
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim in the Greenpeace PDF; 218 GWh (2023) and 984 GWh (2024) match low and mid by the stated convention.

figures.claim: Projected AI chipmaking electricity in 2030 (conservative to ambitious scenarios)
figures.quote: the electricity consumption would be expected to increase to between 11,550 GWh and 37,238 GWh
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; 11,550 and 37,238 GWh match low and high.

figures.claim: AI chipmaking electricity as a share of data-centre electricity in 2024: 0.984 TWh / 415 TWh (IEA, held by Hum) = about 0.24% (our arithmetic)
figures.quote: Global electricity consumption from AI chipmaking increased by more than 350% year on year, from 218 GWh in 2023 to nearly 984 GWh in 2024.
figures.publisher: Greenpeace East Asia; IEA (via Hum's sources)
figures.check_note: Quote on page; 0.984/415 = 0.237%, which rounds to 0.24% (derived arithmetic, correct).

gaps: No chipmaker reports electricity used for AI chips specifically.
The estimate excludes in-house accelerators (Google TPU, AWS Trainium) and general server parts such as CPUs, DRAM and NAND.
No independent, non-advocacy estimate was found to cross-check it.

questions.q: How much CO2 does AI chip manufacturing emit?
questions.evidence_people_ask: No forum links, because the search budget was exhausted. Greenpeace's press release headline on AI chip emissions was widely picked up: https://www.greenpeace.org/eastasia/press/68006/artificial-intelligence-supply-chain-threatens-climate-progress-in-east-asia/
questions.verdict: An estimated 0.45 million tonnes in 2024 from factory electricity, possibly 5 to 17 million tonnes by 2030.
questions.answer: The same Greenpeace and de Vries study estimates that emissions from AI chipmakers' electricity rose from 99,200 t CO2e in 2023 to 453,600 t in 2024. That is about a quarter of one percent of the roughly 180 Mt the IEA links to data centres. Factory electricity is carbon-heavy because fossil fuels supplied 83.1% of Taiwan's power in 2023, 68.6% of Japan's and 58.5% of South Korea's. If those grids stay as they are, 2030 emissions could reach 5.2 to 16.8 Mt. The study counts electricity only, not process gases. It uses grid averages, not companies' green-power purchases.

figures.claim: Emissions from electricity used in AI chipmaking, 2023 to 2024
figures.unit: t CO2e per year (2023 value in low, 2024 value in mid)
figures.quote: rising from 99,200 metric tons of CO₂ equivalent in 2023 to 453,600 metric tons of CO₂ equivalent in 2024
figures.publisher: Greenpeace East Asia (with Alex de Vries)
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim (CO2 subscript normalised); 99,200 and 453,600 t match.

figures.claim: Projected 2030 emissions from AI chipmaking electricity if grid mixes stay the same
figures.quote: ranging from 5.2 to 16.8 million metric tons across conservative, base-case, and ambitious scenarios
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; 5.2 and 16.8 Mt match low and high.

figures.claim: Fossil share of electricity in Taiwan in 2023 (83.1%), with Japan 68.6% and South Korea 58.5%
figures.quote: with 2023 figures showing 83.1% reliance in Taiwan, 68.6% in Japan, and 58.5% in South Korea
figures.publisher: Greenpeace East Asia (citing EPSIS, MOEAEA, METI)
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; Taiwan 83.1% matches mid.

figures.claim: 2024 AI chipmaking emissions vs IEA data-centre CO2: 0.4536 Mt / 180 Mt (held by Hum) = about 0.25% (our arithmetic)
figures.quote: rising from 99,200 metric tons of CO₂ equivalent in 2023 to 453,600 metric tons of CO₂ equivalent in 2024
figures.publisher: Greenpeace East Asia; IEA (via Hum's sources)
figures.check_note: Quote on page; 0.4536/180 = 0.252%, which rounds to 0.25% (derived, correct).

gaps: Emissions from fluorinated process gases at AI-chip fabs are not included in this estimate.
No market-based figure: the authors say reporting differs too much between chipmakers to compute one.

questions.q: How much water does a chip factory use?
questions.evidence_people_ask: No forum links, because the search budget was exhausted. TSMC water use during Taiwan's droughts is a recurring news topic, and Wikipedia's TSMC article cites a World Economic Forum piece on fab water (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSMC). That WEF page returned 403, so I could not read it.
questions.audience: Adults and students who heard chipmaking is thirsty
questions.verdict: A large chip factory can use up to about 38 million litres a day, mostly to make ultrapure water.
questions.answer: The Berlin think tank Interface reports that a large chip factory uses up to 38 million litres (10 million US gallons) of water a day. Most of it goes into making ultrapure water for rinsing wafers. Recycling varies a lot: about 80% in Taiwan, against 10-14% at European factories. The 38 million litres is water taken in, not water that disappears. How much is actually consumed (evaporated or not returned) is less clear. We could not open TSMC's own water data, so there is no TSMC figure here. Water per AI GPU is not published.

figures.claim: Water use of a large semiconductor fab
figures.quote: A large semiconductor fab uses up to 38 million litres (L) (equal to 10 million gallons) per day
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim on the interface-eu page; 38 million L/day matches.

figures.claim: Water recycling rate at fabs in Taiwan (about 80%) vs Europe (10-14%)
figures.quote: Fabs located in Europe have significantly lower water recycling rates (10%–14%) than those located in Taiwan (~80%).
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; Europe 10-14% (low/high) and Taiwan ~80% (mid) match the stated convention.

gaps: TSMC's own water withdrawal and consumption figures: esg.tsmc.com and the investor site returned HTTP 403, so they could not be read.
The reported TSMC Hsinchu figure (over 150,000 tonnes a day, about 10% of city supply) comes via the World Economic Forum, and that page returned 403, so it is unverified.
No water-per-GPU or water-per-wafer figure for AI chips was found from a primary source.
questions.angle: chips: manufacturing energy, water and emissions (TSMC, Nvidia GPUs), embodied carbon

questions.q: How much of Taiwan's electricity does TSMC use?
questions.evidence_people_ask: No forum links, because the search budget was exhausted. The question shows up in policy commentary on Taiwan's grid strain, for example New Lines Institute: https://newlinesinstitute.org/geo-economics/taiwans-semiconductor-sustainability-and-global-implications/
questions.audience: Adults following AI supply-chain and Taiwan energy news
questions.verdict: Roughly 9% in 2023: about 25 TWh of energy, mostly electricity, out of about 277 TWh used in Taiwan.
questions.answer: The New Lines Institute, citing Statista's compilation of TSMC data, says TSMC used nearly 25,000 GWh of energy in 2023, mostly electricity. It quotes Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs for the country's total electricity consumption that year: 276,519 GWh. Dividing gives about 9%. That is our rough arithmetic, and slightly high, because not all of TSMC's energy is electricity. TSMC makes far more than AI chips, so this is not AI's share. Both numbers come to us second-hand: we could not open TSMC's own report or Taiwan's statistics directly.

figures.quote: Electricity was the primary source of the nearly 25,000 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy consumed
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim on the New Lines page, which credits TSMC in 2023; 25,000 GWh matches.

figures.claim: Taiwan total electricity consumption in 2023
figures.quote: In 2023, the industrial sector accounted for more than half (55.3%) of Taiwan's total electricity consumption (276,519 GWh).
figures.publisher: New Lines Institute (citing Taiwan MOEA Energy Statistics Handbook 2023)
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; 276,519 GWh matches.

figures.claim: TSMC share of Taiwan electricity: about 25,000 / 276,519 = about 9% (our arithmetic; an upper bound because TSMC's figure is total energy)
figures.quote: Electricity was the primary source of the nearly 25,000 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy consumed
figures.check_note: Quote on page; 25000/276519 = 9.04%, about 9% (derived, correct).

gaps: TSMC's sustainability report and ESG data (esg.tsmc.com, investor.tsmc.com) returned HTTP 403, so the primary electricity figure and its 2024/2025 values are unverified.
The Taiwan total was read only as quoted by New Lines, not on the MOEA site.
The share of TSMC electricity that goes to AI chips is not published.

questions.q: Do chip factories release greenhouse gases other than CO2?
questions.evidence_people_ask: No forum links, because the search budget was exhausted. Industry explainers such as Interface's report treat fluorinated gases as a standing question about chip emissions: https://www.interface-eu.org/publications/chip-productions-ecological-footprint
questions.verdict: Yes. Fluorinated gases used to etch and clean wafers make up most of a factory's on-site emissions, although electricity is the bigger source overall.
questions.answer: Interface reports that fluorinated gases make up 80-90% of a chip factory's direct, on-site emissions. Some are extremely potent: CHF3 warms the planet 12,400 times as much as the same amount of CO2. NF3 accounts for about 70% of the fluorinated gases used. CF4 is only 11% of use but 32% of the emissions. Even so, Interface says electricity is the biggest single source of chipmaking greenhouse gases. These shares describe chipmaking in general; we found no figure for AI chips specifically.

figures.claim: Fluorinated gases' share of a fab's direct (Scope 1) emissions
figures.quote: account for 80%–90% of direct emissions in a fab.
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; 80% and 90% match low and high.

figures.claim: Global warming potential of CHF3 relative to CO2
figures.quote: CHF3 has a significantly higher GWP of 12,400x.
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; GWP 12,400 matches.

figures.claim: CF4 share of fluorinated-gas use (11%) vs share of fluorinated-gas emissions (32%)
figures.quote: CF4 is low in usage (11%) but emits 32% of all emissions.
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; 11% of usage and 32% of emissions match.

gaps: Global tonnage of fluorinated-gas emissions from semiconductor manufacturing was not sourced.
There is no split of process-gas emissions attributable to AI chips.
The fab-level split between electricity and process gases is not given as a single percentage.

questions.q: How much electronic waste will AI create?
questions.evidence_people_ask: No forum links, because the search budget was exhausted. The Nature Computational Science paper on generative-AI e-waste got wide media attention: its page shows 1,169 Altmetric and 114 citations. https://www.nature.com/articles/s43588-024-00712-6
questions.audience: Adults concerned about hardware turnover and e-waste
questions.verdict: One study estimates 1.2 to 5.0 million tonnes of e-waste from generative-AI hardware in total over 2020-2030.
questions.answer: A 2024 paper in Nature Computational Science modelled the servers behind large language models. It estimated 1.2 to 5.0 million tonnes of e-waste in total between 2020 and 2030, depending on how fast AI grows. The authors say faster hardware replacement and limits on chip imports could push it higher. Keeping servers longer, reusing parts and recycling could cut it by 16-86%. This is a model projection, not a measured tonnage, and it is a total for the decade, not a yearly figure.

figures.claim: Cumulative generative-AI e-waste over 2020-2030 across scenarios
figures.quote: potentially reaching a total accumulation of 1.2–5.0 million tons during 2020–2030, under different future GAI development settings.
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim on the Nature Computational Science page; 1.2 and 5.0 Mt match.

figures.claim: Possible reduction in e-waste from circular economy strategies
figures.quote: the implementation of circular economy strategies along the GAI value chain could reduce e-waste generation by 16–86%.
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim; 16% and 86% match.

gaps: No measured annual tonnage of retired AI servers or GPUs was found.
Actual service lives of AI accelerators in hyperscale data centres are not disclosed in a comparable way.

questions.q: What is Nvidia's carbon footprint, and where does it come from?
questions.evidence_people_ask: No forum links, because the search budget was exhausted. Greenpeace's October 2025 report ranked Nvidia last on AI supply-chain decarbonisation and highlighted its Scope 3 growth: https://www.greenpeace.org/eastasia/press/68382/nvidia-ranks-last-on-ai-supply-chain-decarbonization-greenpeace-report-finds/
questions.audience: Adults and investors-in-general curious about big AI companies' footprints
questions.verdict: Almost all of it is in the supply chain: 10.7 million tonnes in FY2026, against about 10,000 tonnes from Nvidia's own operations (market-based).
questions.answer: Nvidia's FY2026 report covers January 2025 to January 2026. It puts Scope 3 emissions at 10,700,940 t CO2e, up from 6,912,577 t a year earlier. Scope 3 means emissions from its supply chain and other outside activity. Of that, 9,301,735 t is purchased goods and services: mostly chips, memory and assembly by suppliers such as TSMC. Scope 1 and 2 combined came to 10,390 t on a market basis, which counts Nvidia's clean-power purchases. On a location basis, using local grid averages, Scope 2 alone was 308,891 t. The Scope 3 table lists only categories 1-8, so emissions from customers running Nvidia GPUs are not in it. These are company-reported figures, partly estimated.

figures.check_note: Table row verbatim. The columns are FY26, FY25, FY24, so 10,700,940 (FY26) is mid and 6,912,577 (FY25) is low. Correct.

figures.claim: Nvidia Scope 3 Category 1 (purchased goods and services) FY26; about 87% of Scope 3 (9,301,735 / 10,700,940, our arithmetic)
figures.quote: Category 1: Purchased goods and services 9,301,735 6,036,105 3,216,144

figures.claim: Nvidia Scope 1 and 2 (market-based) FY26
figures.quote: Scope 1 and 2, market-based 10,390 9,047 49,442
figures.check_note: Row verbatim; 10,390 FY26 matches.

figures.claim: Nvidia Scope 2 location-based FY26
figures.quote: Scope 2, location-based 308,891 228,378 178,087
figures.check_note: Row verbatim; 308,891 FY26 matches.

gaps: Nvidia does not report Scope 3 Category 11 (use of sold products), even though its target covers use-phase emissions per PFLOP.
How much of Category 1 is AI data-centre GPUs versus gaming and other products is not disclosed.
Prior-year figures were restated, so year-on-year comparisons partly reflect method changes.

questions.q: How long does an AI chip (GPU) last in a data centre?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Tom's Hardware ran a widely shared story on datacenter GPU service life, and readers in its comment thread asked what 'utilization rate' means and how long the chips really last: https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/gpus/datacenter-gpu-service-life-can-be-surprisingly-short-only-one-to-three-years-is-expected-according-to-unnamed-google-architect
questions.audience: Curious adults, gamers and tech readers, investors
questions.verdict: Nobody has published a measured figure. Claims run from 1 to 3 years (one unverified insider) to 5 or 6 years (company accounts).
questions.answer: There is no published, measured average lifespan for AI GPUs. The most quoted short figure is 1 to 3 years at 60-70% utilisation. It comes from one unnamed person said to be a Google architect, and Tom's Hardware says it could not verify who they are. Company figures run longer. Google's life-cycle study of its own TPU chips assumes six years. In their accounts, Amazon now writes off some servers over five years and Meta over 5.5 years. Those are accounting estimates, not how long chips physically survive. 'Lifespan' can also mean when a chip breaks or when it is retired for a faster model, and those are different things.

figures.claim: An unverified Alphabet insider says datacenter GPUs at 60-70% utilisation typically last 1-2 years, 3 at most
figures.quote: With such utilization rates, a GPU will typically survive between one and two years, three years at the most, according to a quote allegedly made by a principal generative AI architect from Alphabet
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim on Tom's Hardware. 1-2 years, 3 at most; the source is an unnamed person and the article says the quote was 'allegedly' made.

figures.claim: Utilisation of AI GPUs at cloud providers (as reported, unverified)
figures.quote: The utilization rates of GPUs for AI workloads in a datacenter run by cloud service providers (CSP) is between 60% and 70%.
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim; 60% to 70% matches.

figures.claim: Google's TPU life-cycle study assumes a six-year life for AI machines
figures.quote: We use a lifespan of six years for AI machines.
figures.publisher: Google (arXiv: Life-Cycle Emissions of AI Hardware)
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim in arXiv 2502.01671 HTML; six years matches.

figures.claim: Meta's accounting life for certain servers and network assets
figures.quote: resulted in an increase in their estimated useful life to 5.5 years, effective beginning fiscal year 2025.
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim in Meta 10-K FY2024; 5.5 years matches.

gaps: No primary, measured average service life for AI GPUs (H100/B200 etc.) found from any operator or Nvidia.
The 1-3 year claim is a second-hand quote from an unverified social-media source; treat as anecdote.
Meta 10-K quote was read via WebFetch's extraction, which may have trimmed the start of the sentence; recheck the exact wording in the filing.

questions.q: How often do AI chips break?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Readers in the Tom's Hardware comment thread argued about whether heat, voltage and constant load wear out datacenter GPUs, and the article leans on Meta's failure data: https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/gpus/datacenter-gpu-service-life-can-be-surprisingly-short-only-one-to-three-years-is-expected-according-to-unnamed-google-architect
questions.verdict: They break often enough to matter. In Meta's biggest training run, faulty GPUs or their memory caused about half of the unplanned stops.
questions.answer: The best public measurement comes from Meta's Llama 3 paper. Meta trained the model on up to 16K H100 GPUs. Over a 54-day stretch it logged 466 job interruptions, and 419 of them were unplanned. Faulty GPUs caused 148 of those stops and GPU memory (HBM3) caused 72. About 78% of the unplanned stops were confirmed or suspected hardware problems. If each failure was a different chip, about 1.3% of the GPUs failed in 54 days, roughly 9% a year. Tom's Hardware reached the same estimate. This is one company and one cluster, early in the chips' life. It is not an industry failure rate.

figures.claim: Job interruptions during a 54-day Llama 3 pre-training snapshot
figures.quote: During a 54-day snapshot period of pre-training, we experienced a total of 466 job interruptions.
figures.publisher: Meta (arXiv: The Llama 3 Herd of Models)
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim in the Llama 3 paper; 466 matches.

figures.claim: Unexpected interruptions
figures.quote: The remaining 419 were unexpected interruptions, which are classified in Table 5.
figures.publisher: Meta (arXiv: The Llama 3 Herd of Models)
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim; 419 matches.

figures.claim: Interruptions from faulty GPUs (148, 30.1%) and HBM3 memory (72, 17.2%)
figures.quote: out of 419 unforeseen disruptions (during a 54-day pre-training snapshot), 148 (30.1%) were instigated by diverse GPU failures (including NVLink fails), whereas 72 (17.2%) were caused by HBM3 memory flops.
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim on Tom's Hardware; 148+72=220 matches.

figures.claim: Share of unexpected interruptions from confirmed or suspected hardware issues
figures.quote: About 78% of unexpected interruptions were attributed to confirmed or suspected hardware issues
figures.publisher: Meta (arXiv: The Llama 3 Herd of Models)
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim in the Llama 3 paper; 78% matches.

figures.claim: Cluster size: up to 16K H100 GPUs (16,384 per Tom's Hardware)
figures.quote: Llama 3 405B is trained on up to 16K H100 GPUs
figures.publisher: Meta (arXiv: The Llama 3 Herd of Models)
figures.check_note: The arXiv quote says 'up to 16K', not 16,384. The figure 16,384 comes from Tom's Hardware ('16,384 Nvidia H100 80GB GPUs'), so it rests on the second source.

figures.claim: Calculated: (148+72)/16,384 = 1.34% in 54 days; x 365/54 = about 9.1% per year, assuming each interruption was a different GPU
figures.quote: out of 419 unforeseen disruptions (during a 54-day pre-training snapshot), 148 (30.1%) were instigated by diverse GPU failures (including NVLink fails), whereas 72 (17.2%) were caused by HBM3 memory flops.
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim. The arithmetic holds: 220/16384 = 1.34%, and x365/54 = 9.08%, which rounds to 9.1. It is a derived figure that assumes each interruption was a different GPU, and the 16,384 comes from a separate Tom's sentence.

figures.claim: Tom's Hardware's own estimate of the annualised H100 failure rate at Meta's rate
figures.quote: If GPUs and their memory keep failing at Meta's rate, then the annualized failure rate of these processors will be around 9%
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim on Tom's Hardware; around 9% matches.

gaps: An interruption is not the same as a permanently dead chip. Some faulty GPUs may have been repaired or reset, and one GPU could cause several interruptions.
No industry-wide or Nvidia-published annualised failure rate for datacenter GPUs found.

questions.q: How much electronic waste will AI create?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The 2024 Nature Computational Science study was widely covered in the news and is a common prompt for 'does AI create e-waste?' questions: https://www.nature.com/articles/s43588-024-00712-6
questions.verdict: One peer-reviewed model puts it at 1.2 to 5.0 million tonnes in total over 2020-2030. That is an estimate from a scenario model, not a measurement.
questions.answer: The main estimate is a 2024 peer-reviewed study in Nature Computational Science. It modelled the e-waste from generative AI, mostly servers for large language models, and found a total of 1.2 to 5.0 million tonnes between 2020 and 2030, depending on how fast AI grows. The study names two things that could push the number up: replacing servers quickly to save running costs, and restrictions on chip imports. It also says reusing, refurbishing and recycling could cut the e-waste by 16% to 86%. Nobody publishes a measured tonnage of AI hardware actually thrown away, so this is a projection.

figures.claim: Cumulative generative-AI e-waste 2020-2030, depending on scenario
figures.quote: potentially reaching a total accumulation of 1.2–5.0 million tons during 2020–2030
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim on the Nature Computational Science page; 1.2-5.0 Mt matches.

figures.claim: Circular-economy strategies could cut generative-AI e-waste
figures.quote: could reduce e-waste generation by 16–86%
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim; 16-86% matches.

gaps: No annual (per-year) 2030 figure was verified on the abstract page; the full paper is paywalled.
No measured tonnage of decommissioned AI hardware from any operator or regulator.

questions.q: Is AI e-waste a big part of the world's electronic waste?
questions.evidence_people_ask: News coverage of the Nature study and of the UN Global E-waste Monitor 2024 led many readers to compare AI hardware waste with phones and household electronics: https://ewastemonitor.info/the-global-e-waste-monitor-2024/
questions.verdict: Not yet. Even the high estimate for a whole decade of AI e-waste is about 8% of what the world threw out in 2022 alone.
questions.answer: The UN-backed Global E-waste Monitor counted a record 62 million tonnes of e-waste worldwide in 2022 and expects 82 million tonnes by 2030. The Nature study estimates 1.2 to 5.0 million tonnes from generative AI across all of 2020-2030. Even the top of that range for the whole decade comes to about 8% of one year's global e-waste. So AI hardware is a small but fast-growing slice. The study's point is about growth and how valuable and recoverable the materials are, not current size. Both figures are estimates. The 2022 total is a modelled global figure, not a weighed one.

figures.claim: Global e-waste generated in 2022
figures.quote: A record 62 million tonnes (Mt) of e-waste was produced in 2022
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim on the GEM 2024 page; 62 Mt matches.

figures.claim: Global e-waste projected for 2030
figures.quote: on track to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030, a further 33% increase from the 2022 figure.
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim; 82 Mt matches.

figures.claim: Calculated: 5.0 Mt (top of 2020-2030 generative-AI range) / 62 Mt (world e-waste in 2022) = about 8%
figures.quote: potentially reaching a total accumulation of 1.2–5.0 million tons during 2020–2030
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim (1.2-5.0 Mt). The calculation holds: 1.2/62 = 1.9%, about 2, and 5/62 = 8.1%, about 8. It compares a cumulative 2020-2030 total with a single year's (2022) e-waste, so it is apples to oranges. The 62 comes from a different source.

gaps: No official figure for data-centre or server e-waste as a share of global e-waste.

questions.q: What happens to old data centre servers? Are they recycled?
questions.evidence_people_ask: In the Tom's Hardware comment thread, readers discuss retired datacenter GPUs such as the Nvidia P100 showing up cheaply on eBay, which raises the question of where retired hardware goes: https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/gpus/datacenter-gpu-service-life-can-be-surprisingly-short-only-one-to-three-years-is-expected-according-to-unnamed-google-architect
questions.verdict: The big clouds say most of it is reused or recycled. These are the companies' own figures, and no independent check was found.
questions.answer: Microsoft says it reused or recycled 92% of its decommissioned servers and components in fiscal 2025, beating its 90% target, and that it runs seven 'Circular Centers'. Google says it took more than 7.5 million components from retired hardware in 2025 to reuse itself. It also says it has resold over 54 million components to other organisations since 2015, 2.6 million of them in 2025. These are company claims, and they count parts or rates, not tonnes. They do not say how much of the hardware is reused whole and how much is shredded for its materials. Smaller operators publish little.

figures.claim: Microsoft reuse and recycling rate for servers and components, FY25
figures.quote: In FY25, Microsoft achieved a 92% reuse and recycling rate for servers and components, exceeding its 90% target for the second consecutive year.
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim in the Microsoft 2026 sustainability report PDF (text extracted); 92% matches.

figures.claim: Google components harvested from decommissioned hardware for internal reuse in 2025
figures.quote: In 2025, we harvested more than 7.5 million components from our decommissioned hardware for internal reuse through our build, upgrade, and spares programs
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim in the Google report PDF; more than 7.5 million matches.

figures.claim: Google components resold to the secondary market 2015-2025 (2.6 million in 2025)
figures.quote: From 2015 to 2025, we've resold more than 54 million hardware components into the secondary market for reuse by other organizations—including 2.6 million in 2025 alone.
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim; more than 54 million (2.6 million in 2025) matches.

gaps: Microsoft and Google report rates and component counts, not tonnes, and don't separate GPUs/AI accelerators from other hardware.
No independent audit of the reuse/recycling figures was found.

These two PDF quotes were read by downloading the PDFs (checksums matched the official links) and extracting the text, not through WebFetch, because WebFetch cannot parse these PDFs. Recheck them before they get checked: "page".
Amazon and Meta reuse rates for servers not sourced.

questions.q: Is AI making companies replace their servers faster?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Investors and tech readers widely debated depreciation after Amazon shortened some server lives in early 2025, and the Tom's Hardware piece ties short GPU lives to how quickly chips pay back their cost: https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/gpus/datacenter-gpu-service-life-can-be-surprisingly-short-only-one-to-three-years-is-expected-according-to-unnamed-google-architect
questions.verdict: The signals are mixed. Amazon cut some server lives from six to five years, citing AI, while Meta lengthened its to 5.5 years.
questions.answer: In its accounts, Amazon is cutting the expected life of some servers and network gear from six years to five, starting January 2025. It blames 'an increased pace of technology development' in AI and machine learning. A year earlier it had raised the figure from five years to six. Meta went the other way, extending certain servers to 5.5 years from 2025. These are accounting estimates of useful life, used to spread out costs. They are not measurements of when hardware is actually scrapped. Faster replacement would mean more e-waste unless the old kit is reused or recycled.

figures.claim: Amazon shortens the useful life of a subset of servers and networking equipment from 6 to 5 years
figures.quote: are changing the useful lives of a subset of our servers and networking equipment, effective January 1, 2025, from six years to five years.
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim in the Amazon 10-K FY2024; six to five years matches.

figures.claim: Amazon's stated reason: the pace of AI/ML technology
figures.quote: These two changes above are due to an increased pace of technology development, particularly in the area of artificial intelligence and machine learning.
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim; there are no numbers to match.

figures.claim: Amazon had raised server life from 5 to 6 years a year earlier
figures.quote: We had previously increased the useful life of our servers from five years to six years effective January 1, 2024.
figures.check_note: Quote is verbatim; five to six years matches.

figures.claim: Meta extends certain servers and network assets to 5.5 years

questions.q: What is PUE, and what is a typical data centre's PUE today?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Not checked with a forum search. The shared web-search budget ran out before this agent could look for Reddit or People-also-ask evidence. PUE is the headline efficiency metric in the Uptime Institute's annual survey and on Google's public efficiency page (https://datacenters.google/efficiency/), which explains it to a general audience. This is indirect evidence of demand only.
questions.audience: Everyday adults and students meeting the term for the first time
questions.verdict: PUE compares a building's total electricity with what its computers use. The industry average is about 1.5.
questions.answer: Power usage effectiveness (PUE) is a facility's total electricity divided by the electricity its IT equipment uses. A PUE of 1.0 would mean nothing goes to cooling, power conversion or lighting. In Uptime Institute's 2025 survey, respondents' average was 1.54. That means about 0.54 kWh of overhead for every 1 kWh of computing, or roughly a third of the total (our arithmetic). The average fell from 2.5 in 2007 to 1.65 in 2014 (measured, from survey responses). PUE measures how efficient the building is. It says nothing about how efficient the computing is or how much water is used. These are self-reported survey figures, not a census of all data centres.

questions.q: Why has data-centre PUE stopped improving?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Uptime Institute ran an article with this question as its headline, 'Global PUEs — are they going anywhere?' (https://journal.uptimeinstitute.com/global-pues-are-they-going-anywhere/). This agent did not verify a forum thread, because the search budget was exhausted.

questions.answer: The global average PUE dropped quickly until about 2014. Since 2020, Uptime says, it has been stuck in the 1.55 to 1.59 band. Uptime gives two reasons. questions.q: How much of a data centre's electricity goes to cooling?

questions.verdict: About 7% in the most efficient big sites, and over 30% in older, less efficient ones.
questions.answer: It depends heavily on the facility. The IEA estimates that cooling takes about 7% of total consumption in efficient hyperscale data centres and over 30% in less efficient enterprise ones. Servers take around 60% on average in modern data centres. The rest goes to storage, networking, power conversion and lighting. These are IEA estimates of consumption, the electricity the building draws, not generation. A site's PUE gives a rough check. At PUE 1.09, overhead (cooling plus everything else) is about 8% of the total. At 1.54 it is about 35% (our arithmetic).
