questions.q: Is liquid cooling better for the environment than air cooling?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Not checked with a forum search, because the search budget was exhausted. Microsoft wrote a general-audience feature about its peer-reviewed Nature study (https://news.microsoft.com/source/features/sustainability/microsoft-quantifies-environmental-impacts-of-datacenter-cooling-from-cradle-to-grave-in-new-nature-study/), which signals public interest.
questions.verdict: A Microsoft-led life-cycle study found lower emissions, energy and water than air cooling. These are modelled results, not measured fleet data.
questions.answer: Liquid cooling carries heat away through cold plates on the chips, or by dipping servers in fluid (immersion). A Microsoft-led life-cycle study, published in Nature, compared these methods with air cooling. It found 15 to 21% lower greenhouse-gas emissions, 15 to 20% lower energy demand and 31 to 52% lower water consumption, counting from manufacture to disposal. These are modelled estimates, by authors at a company that sells cloud services, not measurements across many sites. The study does not say liquid cooling makes AI low-impact overall. Total use still depends on how much computing is built.

questions.q: Are there laws that make data centres be efficient or report their PUE?

questions.verdict: Yes, in Europe. The EU makes larger sites report their energy use, and Germany sets legal PUE limits.

questions.q: Do data centres get paid for their waste heat?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Stockholm Data Parks pitches this directly to operators ('you stop wasting energy and you get paid at the same time'): https://stockholmdataparks.com/ . No public forum evidence collected: the search budget was exhausted.
questions.verdict: In Stockholm, yes, though the money is small next to what the electricity costs.
questions.answer: Stockholm Exergi, the city's heating company, says it pays about two million Swedish kronor (SEK) a year for 1 MW of heat delivered. It says payments are based on what the same heat would cost it to make in its own plants, and they change with outdoor temperature. If 1 MW were delivered every hour of the year (8,760 MWh), that would be roughly 230 SEK per MWh (our rough arithmetic). In practice delivery varies, so treat this as an order of magnitude only. Prices in other cities were not found.

questions.q: Isn't server heat too cool to heat a house? How does it work?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Wikipedia's Data center article says 'It is very difficult to reuse the heat generated by air-cooled data centers', which readers question: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_center . No forum evidence collected: the search budget was exhausted.
questions.verdict: On its own it is lukewarm. Heat pumps raise its temperature, and the heat pumps use electricity too.
questions.answer: Air leaving server halls is warm, but not hot enough for city heating pipes. So operators cool the data hall with heat pumps instead of ordinary chillers, Stockholm Exergi explains, and the captured heat goes into the district-heating network. A 2020 strategy+business article on Stockholm says the heat pumps can raise the waste heat to about 85 °C. The heat pumps consume electricity themselves. We did not find a sourced figure for how much, so the net energy gain is not stated here. Liquid-cooled AI servers may give off hotter water, which could make this easier, but we found no solid figure for that.

questions.q: Does the EU make data centres reuse their waste heat?
questions.evidence_people_ask: It is written into EU law (Energy Efficiency Directive 2023/1791), so lawmakers and industry asked it directly: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/1791/oj/eng . No public forum evidence collected: the search budget was exhausted.
questions.verdict: Partly. Big data centres must use their waste heat unless they can show it isn't technically or economically feasible.
questions.answer: The EU's recast Energy Efficiency Directive (2023) says EU countries must make sure data centres with a total rated energy input above 1 MW use their waste heat, or other heat-recovery options, unless they show that is not technically or economically feasible. Separately, from 15 May 2024 and every year after, operators of data centres with at least 500 kW of IT power must publish energy information listed in the directive. Because of the feasibility exception, the law does not guarantee heat is reused. We found no EU-wide figure for how much heat is actually reused.

questions.q: What does Germany require new data centres to do with their heat?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Set out in Germany's Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG §11): https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/enefg/__11.html . No public forum evidence collected: the search budget was exhausted.
questions.audience: Adults in Germany and Europe, policy readers
questions.verdict: New German data centres must reuse a rising minimum share of their energy: 10%, then 15%, then 20%.
questions.answer: Germany's Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG, section 11) sets minimum shares of 'reused energy', measured with the standard DIN EN 50600-4-6. Data centres starting operation from 1 July 2026 must reach at least 10%. Those starting from 1 July 2027 must plan for at least 15%, and those from 1 July 2028 for at least 20%. The share has to be met as an annual average within two years of starting operation. This is a legal requirement, not a measurement. We found no data yet on whether it is being met.

questions.q: If the heat is reused, does that cancel out a data centre's footprint?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Fortum's own headline claim of CO2 savings ('reduce about 400,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions annually') invites this question: https://www.fortum.com/media/2022/03/fortum-and-microsoft-announce-worlds-largest-collaboration-heat-homes-services-and-businesses-sustainable-waste-heat-new-data-centre-region . No forum evidence collected: the search budget was exhausted.
questions.verdict: No. It puts heat that would be wasted to use, but the electricity is still consumed.
questions.answer: Reusing heat does not reduce a data centre's electricity use. The electricity is consumed either way, and the heat pumps add a little more. What reuse can do is replace other heat sources, such as fossil fuels burned in heating plants. Fortum forecast that its Microsoft scheme would cut about 400,000 tonnes of CO2 a year. That is a company estimate, and the real saving depends on what heat it replaces. Where the heat would otherwise come from clean sources, the saving is smaller. Meta likewise frames Odense in homes heated, not as a cut to its electricity use.

figures.quote: and reduce about 400,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions annually.
figures.check_note: Fortum page: 'and reduce about 400,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions annually.' This is a forecast.

gaps: Independent verification of Fortum's 400,000 t CO2 estimate and its baseline.
Heat-pump electricity use in these schemes.
Lifecycle or peer-reviewed assessment of the net CO2 benefit of data-centre heat reuse.

questions.q: How much of Ireland's electricity do data centres use now?
questions.evidence_people_ask: National news covers this every year when the CSO publishes, e.g. the Irish Times on the CRU decision says data centres use 'one-fifth' of all electricity: https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2025/12/12/new-data-centres-must-generate-and-supply-electricity-to-wider-market-regulator-rules/ . The web search budget ran out during this run, so no forum or PQ threads were collected.
questions.verdict: Almost a quarter: 23% of metered electricity in 2025, up from 5% in 2015.
questions.answer: Ireland's statistics office (CSO) measured 7,663 GWh (about 7.7 TWh) of metered electricity going to data centres in 2025. That is 10% more than in 2024 and 23% of all metered electricity, up from 5% in 2015. Use by everyone else rose only 2% that year. These are measured meter readings of consumption, not estimates. For scale, 7.7 TWh is about 1.6% of the IEA's estimate for all data centres worldwide in 2025 (485 TWh), and it all sits in one small country. SEAI, which counts demand a little differently, put the 2024 share at 21.2%.

questions.q: Is there a ban or moratorium on new data centres in Dublin?
questions.evidence_people_ask: People widely call it a 'de facto moratorium'. EirGrid published a 'Data Centre Constrained Area Overview' (May 2026) to explain where connections are possible: https://www.eirgrid.ie/publications/data-centre-constrained-area-overview-document . The search budget ran out, so no forum or PQ links were collected.
questions.audience: Irish public, local residents, tech workers
questions.verdict: There is no formal ban, but since late 2021 new Dublin grid connections have been nearly impossible, and Dublin is still treated as constrained.
questions.answer: There was never a legal ban. In 2021 the regulator (CRU direction CRU/21/124) told the grid operator to connect new data centres only if they could bring onsite generation or storage at least equal to their demand. EirGrid reports that only one new data centre won a contract under that rule. Almost all the extra load still to come was contracted in greater Dublin before the rule. A new CRU policy (December 2025) replaced it. EirGrid still says Dublin has serious short-circuit limits, and that new generator connections in greater Dublin 'cannot be accommodated' until 400 kV reinforcements are built.

questions.q: What are Ireland's new rules for data centres connecting to the grid?

EirGrid then published applicant guidance, which shows industry and public demand for clarity.
questions.audience: Engaged citizens, students of policy, industry newcomers
questions.verdict: New data centres must bring their own dispatchable power or storage and must match at least 80% of yearly use with new Irish renewables within six years.
questions.answer: The CRU's Large Energy Users Connection Policy (CRU/2025236, December 2025) applies to new data centres of 1 MVA or more. Each must provide dispatchable generation or storage, on site or nearby, big enough to cover its maximum import capacity. It must also show how it will meet at least 80% of its annual electricity with additional renewable power generated in Ireland. Existing wind or solar farms do not count. It gets a six-year glide path from switch-on to reach the 80%. The grid operators also check whether the site is in a constrained area. These are rules, not results. None of it has been measured yet.

questions.q: Could data centres cause blackouts in Ireland?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Grid alerts and blackout fears are a recurring topic in Irish news. questions.verdict: Ireland's supply margin is officially below standard until 2028, mainly because new power plants and an interconnector are late. Data centres add load and some stability risks.
questions.answer: EirGrid's adequacy study expects Ireland to miss its reliability standard (3 hours of expected shortfall a year) from 2026 to 2028. For 2026 it models 71.6 hours. That is a model forecast, not hours of actual blackouts. EirGrid blames late new capacity and the delayed Celtic Interconnector, and expects the position to recover from 2029. Separately, EirGrid reports that data centres have suddenly cut their demand during voltage dips, which shakes grid frequency, and that the 'oscillating demand' of AI data centres could add risk. New data centres must now bring their own dispatchable power, so EirGrid does not expect them to worsen supply security.

questions.q: Are data centres holding back Ireland's renewable electricity targets?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Recurring theme in Irish climate debate. The RTÉ Prime Time piece covers officials asking 'Is it housing or is it AI?': https://www.rte.ie/news/primetime/2025/0821/1529518-govt-warned-of-rising-household-bills-as-data-centres-strain-grid/
questions.verdict: Partly. SEAI names fast-growing demand, mostly from data centres, as one of three reasons Ireland's renewable share has stalled near 40%.
questions.answer: Renewables supplied 41.3% of Ireland's electricity in 2024. The target is 80% by 2030, and SEAI's most optimistic projection reaches 68%. SEAI says the share has hardly moved in five years for three reasons. Wind output has plateaued, the calculation method changed, and demand has risen faster than new renewables are built. Data centres caused 88.2% of Ireland's demand growth since 2015. So every new wind farm has to cover new load as well as replace fossil power. That is why the new rules require data centres to add new Irish renewables. All figures here are measured, except the projection.

questions.q: Why did so many data centres end up in Dublin?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A frequent explainer question, answered in part by EirGrid's 2026 constrained-area document: https://www.eirgrid.ie/publications/data-centre-constrained-area-overview-document . No forum links were collected because the search budget ran out.
questions.verdict: Partly because of a strong high-voltage grid around Dublin built in the 1970s and 80s. Business factors also matter but are not sourced here.
questions.answer: EirGrid's explanation is about infrastructure. Dublin always had more people and industry, so in the 1970s and 1980s it got many 220 kV and 400 kV lines. Two 400 kV lines from Moneypoint power station arrived in the 1980s. That spare capacity let Ireland contract over 2 GW of data centres without big new grid work. It is now used up. Ireland's whole grid is small, with a peak of about 7.5 GW, which is less than greater London's demand. Other reasons often given, such as tax, climate, connectivity and US tech firms' EU headquarters, are not sourced here.

questions.q: What rules does Germany (and so Frankfurt) set for data centres' efficiency and green power?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Indirect: Germany's Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG) is the main law operators in Frankfurt must follow, and the European Commission's 2026 data-centre report refers to its PUE targets. Forum evidence was not gathered because the search budget ran out.
questions.audience: German readers, engineering students, IT professionals
questions.verdict: Germany's Energy Efficiency Act caps energy overhead, requires 100% renewable electricity from 2027, and makes new centres reuse some waste heat.
questions.answer: Germany's Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG, §11) sets legal limits. Centres opened from 1 July 2026 must reach a PUE of 1.2 or better within two years. PUE is total energy divided by the IT equipment's energy, so 1.2 means 20% overhead. Existing centres must reach 1.5 from July 2027 and 1.3 from July 2030. Electricity must be 50% renewable from 2024 and 100% from 2027. Often this is met with certificates on paper rather than direct supply. New centres must plan to reuse at least 10% of their energy as heat, rising to 15% and 20% for later openings, with some exemptions.

questions.q: What do EU rules make data centres report, and can the public see it?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The European Commission keeps a reporter guide and FAQ (dated 17 Sept 2026) for this obligation, which shows operators keep asking (https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficiency-targets-directive-and-rules/energy-efficiency-directive/energy-performance-data-centres_en).
questions.verdict: Data centres of 500 kW or more must report energy and water data every year, but the public only sees national and EU totals.
questions.answer: Under the EU Energy Efficiency Directive (2023/1791, Article 12), owners and operators of data centres with at least 500 kW of installed IT power must report energy-performance data every year. The directive set 15 May 2024 as the first date, and the delegated regulation moved the first report to 15 September 2024, then 15 May 2025 and yearly after that. The data are published only in aggregate, at national and EU level. Figures for individual sites stay confidential. Article 26(6) also requires centres above 1 MW of rated energy input to use their waste heat, unless that is shown to be not technically or economically feasible.

questions.q: Is the EU trying to limit data centres or build more of them?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Indirect: the Commission's Cloud and AI Development Act page and the 2026 rating-scheme consultation both invited public feedback (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cloud-and-ai-development-act).
questions.audience: EU citizens, policy students, tech readers
questions.verdict: Both: the EU wants to at least triple capacity while adding a rating scheme and, later, minimum performance standards.
questions.answer: The EU is pulling in two directions at once. Its proposed Cloud and AI Development Act aims to at least triple the EU's data-centre capacity within 5 to 7 years, partly by making permits and access to energy, land and water easier. It is a proposal, not yet law. On the efficiency side, the Commission proposed a common rating scheme on 21 September 2026 to make energy and water use more transparent. It plans minimum performance standards, with a final proposal planned for Q2 2027. National and city limits, like those in the Netherlands and Amsterdam, stay in place alongside these EU plans.

questions.q: How much of Singapore's electricity do data centres use?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Singapore MPs have asked this in Parliament more than once. In July 2021 Shawn Huang asked about data-centre carbon emissions and energy use (https://www.mddi.gov.sg/newsroom/mci-response-pq-data-carbon-emissions-data-centres-sg/). In February 2026 Elysa Chen asked for the total number and load capacity of data centres (https://www.mddi.gov.sg/newsroom/mddi-s-response-to-pq-on-data-on-total-number-and-load-capacity-of-data-centres-in-singapore/).
questions.verdict: About 7% in 2020, the latest official share. Capacity has grown since, but no newer share has been published.
questions.answer: The government's last published figure is for 2020. Data centres used about 3.40 TWh that year, roughly 7% of the electricity Singapore consumed, up from 5.3% (2.75 TWh) in 2019. These are measured consumption figures. In February 2026 the government said total data-centre capacity was over 1.4 GW across more than 70 facilities. Capacity is the most a site can draw, not what it actually uses, so this does not tell you current consumption. For scale, Singapore used 57 TWh of electricity in total in 2023 (Ember). Hum has not found an official share for any year after 2020.

questions.q: Why did Singapore stop building data centres, and is there a limit now?
questions.evidence_people_ask: In July 2024 MP He Ting Ru asked about the '2019-2022 moratorium' (https://www.mddi.gov.sg/newsroom/pq-on-advancements-in-data-centre-efficiency-by-singapore-companies/). In September 2026 Poh Li San asked whether the 300 MW baseline will be reviewed because of AI (https://www.mddi.gov.sg/newsroom/mddi-response-to-pq-on-future-data-centre-capacity-plans-in-support-of-ai-adoption/).
questions.verdict: Singapore paused new data centres from 2019 to 2022 to work out how to grow sustainably. It now gives out capacity through competitive calls, and has not published a hard cap.
questions.answer: The government calls it a three-year pause in the growth of the industry, imposed to study how that growth could be managed sustainably. After the pause, it gave capacity through a pilot call for applications in 2022 instead of approving every request. Four operators won that round and committed to more efficient designs. A second call picked four more proposals, announced in August 2026. MPs have repeatedly asked about the 300 MW of extra capacity in the 2024 Green Data Centre Roadmap. In both 2026 answers the government gave no new MW figure and no cap. It said only that it would keep reviewing the need for more capacity.

questions.q: What powers Singapore's data centres? Is it clean?

questions.verdict: Mostly natural gas. About 92% of Singapore's electricity came from gas in 2025, and renewables supplied about 6%.
questions.answer: Singapore's grid runs almost entirely on imported natural gas. The IEA estimates gas supplied about 92% of electricity in 2025, down from 94% in 2024, and renewables about 6%, rising to 8% by 2030 (a forecast). So a data centre on the grid is mostly gas-powered, whatever certificates it buys. Singapore plans to import low-carbon electricity from its neighbours. The IEA cites a target of 6 GW of import capacity by 2035, with the first Indonesia link expected around 2029. The government projects peak demand rising from 8.2 GW in 2025 to as much as 11.9 GW in 2032. It has not said how much of that comes from data centres.

questions.q: How much power do Johor's and Malaysia's data centres actually use?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Malaysian press coverage reprinted by MIDA asks whether there is enough power for the boom, e.g. 'Malaysia well-equipped to meet power needs of data centres, says TNB' (https://www.mida.gov.my/mida-news/malaysia-well-equipped-to-meet-power-needs-of-data-centres-says-tnb-president-ceo/) and 'Malaysia's data centre boom: Johor emerges as a regional powerhouse' (https://www.mida.gov.my/mida-news/malaysias-data-centre-boom-johor-emerges-as-a-regional-powerhouse/).

questions.answer: The national utility TNB reports that at December 2025 data centres drew 850 MW of actual load. Peninsular Malaysia's peak demand in 2025 was 21,049 MW, so data-centre load was roughly 4% of it. Most of this is in Johor, which holds 78.6% of Malaysia's operational IT capacity according to the New Straits Times. If 850 MW ran all year it would be about 7.4 TWh, roughly 5.6% of TNB's Peninsular sales. This is Hum's upper-end estimate, not a measured figure.

questions.answer: Ember projects that Malaysian data centres will go from 9 TWh in 2024 to 68 TWh in 2030, about 30% of national power consumption. questions.q: How much electricity do China's data centres use?
questions.evidence_people_ask: I had no web searches left this turn, so I could not collect forum or People-also-ask evidence. Indirect evidence: the IEA's Energy and AI report breaks out China as its own headline region because readers and policymakers ask for the comparison (https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai/executive-summary).
questions.audience: Curious adults and students comparing countries
questions.verdict: About a quarter of the world's data-centre electricity, roughly 100 TWh in 2024, which is only about 1% of China's own very large demand.
questions.answer: The IEA estimates that China accounted for 25% of global data-centre electricity consumption in 2024, second to the United States at 45%. Applied to the IEA's world total of 415 TWh, that is roughly 100 TWh (our calculation). This is consumption, not generation. China's grid is huge, though: its gross electricity demand was approaching 10,000 TWh at the end of 2024, so data centres were about 1% of it (again our calculation). The IEA treats data centres and 5G as one of several drivers of China's demand growth, alongside clean-tech manufacturing, air conditioning and EVs. questions.q: Did DeepSeek really use much less energy than American AI models?
questions.evidence_people_ask: DeepSeek's launch in January 2025 set off wide public debate about whether cheap Chinese models reduce AI's energy use. MIT Technology Review ran an explainer framed around this exact question (https://www.technologyreview.com/2025/01/31/1110776/deepseek-might-not-be-such-good-news-for-energy-after-all/).
questions.verdict: Training took far fewer GPU hours, but answering questions can use more energy, because its reasoning model writes long answers.
questions.answer: DeepSeek reported that its V3 model needed 2.788 million H800 GPU hours for its full training run. Meta reported 30.84 million H100 GPU hours for Llama 3.1 405B, so DeepSeek used about 9% as many (our arithmetic). This is a company claim covering the final run, and the chips differ. Training is only part of the story. In early tests reported by MIT Technology Review, DeepSeek's reasoning model used 41% more energy than a Meta 70B model on one prompt, and 87% more across 40 prompts, mainly because it wrote much longer answers. Efficiency per model does not mean less total energy if usage grows.

questions.verdict: India has a huge share of the world's internet users but little of its data-centre capacity, and companies are investing to close that gap.
questions.answer: The IEA says emerging and developing economies other than China have 50% of the world's internet users but less than 10% of global data-centre capacity. Google's plan for a roughly 1 GW campus in Visakhapatnam has been reported, but Hum could not confirm it from Google's own page in this pass. questions.q: Is India's electricity getting cleaner fast enough to offset data-centre growth?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Ember's 2026 review headlines India's first fall in fossil power this century (https://ember-energy.org/latest-insights/global-electricity-review-2026/). Forum evidence could not be checked because the search limit was reached.
questions.verdict: It is getting cleaner. In 2025, fossil power fell for the first time this century, but coal still supplies about 71%.
questions.answer: In 2025, India's fossil-fuel generation fell by 52 TWh (-3.3%), driven by record solar and wind growth, strong hydro and slow demand growth (measured, Ember). Solar met 9.4% of demand, and wind and solar together 14%. India also installed more new solar capacity than the United States for the first time. But 2025 was a low-demand year. The IEA expects demand to grow about 6.4% a year to 2030, so whether clean power keeps up is a forecast question. Coal still made about 71% of electricity.

questions.q: Do data centres in India run on renewable energy?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Company renewable claims are a recurring theme in Indian coverage, and Wikipedia's Visakhapatnam article reports about $2bn of the Google project as renewable infrastructure. No reader-question URL could be checked because the search limit was reached.
questions.verdict: Unknown in aggregate. Companies make claims, but no independent India-wide figure was found, and the grid they connect to is about 71% coal.
questions.answer: Hum found no measured, India-wide share of data-centre electricity coming from renewables. Individual operators announce green power deals, but these are company claims, often based on annual contracts or certificates rather than hour-by-hour supply. The grid behind them averaged about 671 g CO2e/kWh in 2025, with coal at about 71%. So on location-based accounting, a typical Indian data centre's power is carbon-heavy unless it is physically matched with clean supply. Hum's existing certificates and offsets studies explain why a market-based 'green' claim can differ from the grid reality.

questions.q: How much of Virginia's electricity do data centres use?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Pew Research Center wrote a reader explainer, 'What we know about energy use at US data centers amid the AI boom' (Oct 2025), and its first state figure is Virginia's share: https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/10/24/what-we-know-about-energy-use-at-us-data-centers-amid-the-ai-boom/ . The web search budget ran out during this run, so no forum threads were collected.
questions.audience: US residents, especially Virginians; students; journalists
questions.verdict: About a quarter: roughly 26% of the electricity used in Virginia in 2023, by EPRI's estimate.
questions.answer: The Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) estimates that Virginia's data centres used about 33.9 TWh in 2023, which is 25.6% of all electricity consumed in the state. This is a share of consumption, not of generation. Virginia also buys power from other states, so its share of in-state generation would be a different number. The 2023 figure is a modelled estimate, not a metered count, because no US agency publishes measured data-centre use by state. That makes Virginia the most data-centre-heavy state by far. The next highest shares in EPRI's table are North Dakota (about 15%) and Nebraska, Iowa and Oregon (about 11 to 12%).

questions.verdict: Only about 5% in 2023, by EPRI's estimate. Texas's large-load growth is mostly crypto mining, not only AI.
questions.answer: EPRI estimates that Texas data centres used about 21.8 TWh in 2023, which is 4.6% of the state's electricity consumption. questions.audience: General public, students, local residents near proposed sites
questions.verdict: Nobody publishes an official yearly figure. What is known is capacity: about 1.6 to 1.8 GW of computer load.
questions.answer: The UK government does not publish a yearly electricity figure for data centres. Its energy forecasts fold them into the wider IT sector. What it does publish is capacity, meaning how much computer equipment the buildings can power at once. A government estimate puts the colocation sites in Great Britain at 1.6 GW in autumn 2024, and about two-thirds of that is in London. A government evidence annex puts it at around 1.8 GW across about 330 data centres. If 1.8 GW of computers ran flat out all year, they would use about 15.8 TWh, roughly 5% of the UK's 319 TWh of electricity demand. That number is a ceiling for the computers alone, not a measurement: real sites run below full load but also need power for cooling.

figures.quote: Total IT power: 1.6 gigawatts (GW)
figures.check_note: Quote is on the page: 'Total IT power: 1.6 gigawatts (GW)', autumn 2024 colocation only. 1.6 matches.

figures.check_note: Quote found in the compute evidence annex PDF (text extracted). 1.8 GW and about 330 data centres match.

figures.quote: The Department’s published energy demand forecasts do not separately identify or report electricity demand from data centres.
figures.check_note: Quote matches the answer text of WQ 1922602 exactly.

figures.claim: Total UK electricity demand 2024
figures.quote: around 0.6 per cent of total UK electricity demand, which was 319 TWh in 2024.
figures.check_note: Quote found in the follow-up report PDF. 319 TWh in 2024 matches.

figures.claim: Upper bound if 1.8 GW of IT load ran at 100% all year: 1.8 GW x 8,760 h = 15.8 TWh, about 5% of 319 TWh (computers only, no cooling, no allowance for real utilisation)
figures.quote: Around 1.8GW of UK’s IT load (power capacity) is currently used to power around 330 data centres around the country.
figures.check_note: The quote (1.8 GW) is on the page. 15.8 TWh is Hum's calculation: 1.8 x 8.76 = 15.77 TWh, about 4.9% of 319. The source does not state it, so it should be labelled as derived.

questions.q: What are the UK's AI Growth Zones and where are they?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Lords question HL3627 (Sep 2026) asks about calls for a moratorium on data centres outside designated AI Growth Zones. Q111668 asks how many jobs each AI Growth Zone will create: https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions/1943704
questions.audience: General public, residents in Oxfordshire, Wales, North East England and Scotland
questions.verdict: They are government-backed sites for big AI data centres. Five had been named by February 2026.
questions.answer: AI Growth Zones are places the government picks for large AI data centres. Projects there get faster planning, priority for grid connections and, from 2027, cheaper electricity in some regions. The idea first appeared in the January 2025 AI Opportunities Action Plan. By February 2026 five had been named: Oxfordshire (Culham), North Wales, South Wales, North East England and Lanarkshire in Scotland. The government's goal is several sites that can each take at least 500 MW by 2030, with at least one above 1 GW. In Lanarkshire, the developer DataVita says it plans more than 500 MW of on-site power generation. That is the company's plan, not something that has been built.

figures.claim: Number and names of AI Growth Zones as of Feb 2026
figures.quote: It joins a stable of 5 AI Growth Zones announced in the 12 months since the launch of the AI Opportunities Action Plan, joining Oxfordshire, North and South Wales, and the North East of England
figures.check_note: Quote matches the Lanarkshire press release. It gives 5 zones: Oxfordshire, North Wales, South Wales, North East, plus Lanarkshire.

figures.claim: Target size of AI Growth Zone sites by 2030
figures.quote: Our goal is to establish a core group of nationally significant sites, each capable of serving at least 500MW of demand by 2030, with at least one AI Growth Zone scaling to more than 1GW by 2030.
figures.check_note: Quote found in the UK Compute Roadmap. 500 MW per site and over 1 GW for at least one zone match low 500 and high 1000. Note the source says more than 1 GW.

figures.claim: Lanarkshire developer's planned on-site generation
figures.quote: DataVita planning to include the generation of more than 500MW of on-site power to drive AI breakthroughs in the next 4 years.
figures.check_note: Quote found. The release says 'more than 500MW' of on-site power, so mid 500 is a lower bound.

figures.claim: Origin of AI Growth Zones
figures.quote: Establish 'AI Growth Zones' (AIGZs) to facilitate the accelerated build out of AI data centres.
figures.check_note: Quote found in the AI Opportunities Action Plan.

gaps: The government publishes no per-zone power capacity (MW) or expected electricity use for each zone.
Zones named after February 2026 could not be confirmed: the gov.uk collection page was last updated Nov 2025, and web search was unavailable.

questions.q: How much data centre capacity does the UK want by 2030, and could the grid cope?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Q8970 (Jun 2026) asked for 'the annual electricity consumption associated with 6GW of AI-capable data centre capacity'. Lords HL2805 asked for 'the additional electricity needed to power data centres by 2035': https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions/1914988 ; https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions/1936937
questions.verdict: The government wants at least 6 GW by 2030, three times today's capacity. The grid operator says that much is manageable.
questions.answer: The government's Compute Roadmap forecasts the UK will need at least 6 GW of AI-capable data centre capacity by 2030, three times what exists today. The 2035 demand scenarios behind it (McKinsey modelling for DSIT) run from 7.4 to 13.6 GW, with 9.6 GW in the main case. At a 2026 meeting of the government's AI Energy Council, NESO, which runs Britain's grid, said 6 GW fits its Clean Power 2030 plans and is manageable, but going further needs more work. Asked how much electricity 6 GW would use in a year, ministers gave no number and called it uncertain. For scale: 6 GW running flat out all year would be about 53 TWh, around 16% of 2024 UK demand. That is a ceiling, not a forecast.

figures.claim: UK need for AI-capable data centre capacity by 2030 (government forecast)
figures.quote: We forecast that the UK will need at least 6GW of AI-capable data centre capacity by 2030 – a threefold increase on the data centre capacity that is available in the UK today.
figures.check_note: Quote found in the Compute Roadmap. 'At least 6GW' matches mid 6.

figures.claim: UK compute demand 2035, IT load scenarios (McKinsey for DSIT)
figures.quote: The main scenario is for total compute demand to grow from 1.8GW in 2024 to 9.6GW by 2035 (Table 1), driven by steadily increasing AI integration across sectors. However, this could vary between 7.4GW and 13.6GW.
figures.check_note: Quote found in the annex PDF. 7.4, 9.6 and 13.6 GW match low, mid and high.

figures.claim: NESO view of 6 GW
figures.quote: NESO confirmed that 6GW is broadly aligned with Clean Power 2030 planning and is manageable, but that scaling beyond this would require further work.
figures.check_note: Quote found in the AI Energy Council minutes of 13 April 2026.

figures.claim: Government declines to estimate annual consumption of 6 GW
figures.quote: Future electricity demand for data centres is uncertain because different scenarios for data centre capacity, efficiency, utilisation and ramp-up rate translate into varying annual electricity consumption.
figures.check_note: Quote matches the answer text of WQ 1914988.

figures.claim: Ceiling: 6 GW x 8,760 h = 52.6 TWh, about 16% of 2024 UK demand of 319 TWh (assumes 100% load all year; not a forecast)
figures.quote: We forecast that the UK will need at least 6GW of AI-capable data centre capacity by 2030
figures.check_note: The quote (6 GW) is on the Roadmap. 52.6 TWh is Hum's calculation: 6 x 8.76 = 52.56 TWh, about 16.5% of 319. The source does not state it.

gaps: No official TWh projection for UK data centres in 2030 or 2035; DESNZ says it is testing scenarios but has not published one.
NESO's own data-centre demand scenarios (FES 2025) could not be read (HTTP 403).

questions.q: Are data centres clogging up the National Grid connection queue?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Q26554 (Sep 2026) asked how many data centres have requested grid connections and whether this delays housing, manufacturing and low-carbon generation. Q8370 asked what share of the demand queue is data centres: https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions/1937341 ; https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions/1914360
questions.audience: General public, housing and business developers, local councils
questions.verdict: Yes. Data centres have asked for about 73 GW of connections, more than Britain's whole peak demand of about 45 GW.
questions.answer: NESO data quoted by ministers shows 72.8 GW of grid capacity set aside for data centres in Britain's connection queue, counting both the high-voltage transmission network and local networks. On the transmission network alone, data centres hold about 60 GW, around three-quarters of all demand waiting to connect. Britain's peak demand is about 45 GW. Many of these are requests, not real projects: in a voluntary NESO survey, 140 data centre developers reported being in the pipeline, which shows intent rather than confirmed delivery. The government says the oversubscription is delaying every kind of demand project. It has consulted on raising financial requirements and removing speculative applications.

figures.claim: Capacity allocated to data centres in the GB connection queue (transmission + distribution), 2025 data
figures.quote: Data collected in 2025 and published by the National Energy System Operator shows 72.8 GW of capacity allocated to data centres in the GB connection queue across transmission and distribution.
figures.publisher: UK Parliament written answer (DESNZ) citing NESO, Q26554
figures.check_note: Quote matches WQ 1937341. 72.8 GW matches.

figures.claim: Data centres in the transmission demand queue and share of it
figures.quote: Data supplied by the National Energy System Operator shows around 60GW of capacity allocated to data centres in the transmission queue. This represents around three quarters of the total demand connections queue, at transmission level.
figures.publisher: UK Parliament written answer (DESNZ) citing NESO, Q8370
figures.check_note: Quote matches WQ 1914360. About 60 GW, around three quarters of the transmission demand queue.

figures.claim: Total demand in connections queue vs GB peak demand
figures.quote: 125GW of demand currently sits in the connections queue – compared to a peak of approx. 45GW.
figures.check_note: Quote found in the minutes. A peak of about 45 GW matches mid 45; the 125 GW queue is also stated.

figures.claim: Prospective data centres self-reporting to NESO, and number in Scotland
figures.quote: 140 prospective data centres self-reported their presence in the pipeline for connections. 19 of these were located in Scotland. However, these responses were voluntary and represent developer intent rather than confirmed deliverability.
figures.check_note: Quote matches WQ 1892511. 140 prospective data centres, 19 of them in Scotland.

figures.claim: Data-centre queue vs peak demand: 72.8 / 45 = about 1.6 times
figures.quote: 125GW of demand currently sits in the connections queue – compared to a peak of approx. 45GW.
figures.check_note: The quote (45 GW peak) is in the minutes, but 72.8 GW comes from WQ 1937341, not from this page. The ratio is 72.8/45 = 1.62, so 1.6 is Hum's own calculation across two sources.

gaps: No published count of individual data-centre projects in the queue; DESNZ says it cannot provide one.
Results of NESO's mandatory March 2026 information request to validate the queue were not found.
The government's response to its March 2026 data-centre connections consultation was still pending at the time of these answers.

questions.q: Will AI data centres make my UK electricity bill go up?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Q96026 asked about the impact of AI data-centre demand on electricity prices. Q26555 asked how much of the cost of network reinforcement consumers will pay. Lords HL16730 asked how to ensure data-centre demand 'does not increase costs for consumers': https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions/1858768 ; https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions/1937342
questions.verdict: Unknown. The government says its data-centre discounts cost other bill payers nothing, but it does not track network costs caused by data centres.
questions.answer: From April 2027, subject to legislation, data centres in some AI Growth Zones will pay less for electricity: up to £24/MWh less in Scotland, £16 in Cumbria and £14 in the North East. The government says the discount comes from savings when data centres use power that would otherwise be wasted, so it adds no cost for other bill payers. That is the government's own claim; no independent check was found. Ministers also say they do not track the cost of grid upgrades needed to connect new data centres. Ofgem, the energy regulator, decides how those costs are split between developers, network companies and consumers. No published estimate of the effect on household bills was found.

figures.claim: AI Growth Zone electricity cost reduction from April 2027
figures.quote: From April 2027, subject to legislative timetables, data centres in AI Growth Zones will see a reduction in electricity costs of up to: £24/MWh in Scotland £16/MWh in Cumbria £14/MWh in the North East, with a review point in 2030.
figures.check_note: Quote found on Delivering AI Growth Zones. £24, £16 and £14 per MWh; low 14 and high 24 match.

figures.claim: Government claim of no extra cost to other bill payers
figures.quote: the design of the approach means there will be no additional cost for other electricity billpayers.
figures.check_note: Quote found on Delivering AI Growth Zones.

figures.claim: Government does not track network reinforcement costs for data centres
figures.quote: Government is not tracking the network reinforcement cost data associated specifically with new data centres.
figures.check_note: Quote matches WQ 1937342.

gaps: No independent (Ofgem, NAO or academic) estimate found of how data-centre growth affects UK household bills.
No estimate of total network investment attributable to data centres; DESNZ declined to publish one.

questions.q: Why does the government want data centres in Scotland and the North rather than London?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Lords HL5757 asked about putting data centres near Scottish wind farms 'that have previously been turned off due to the electricity grid being unable to handle excess generation'. Q26527 asked about steering data centres to areas with spare renewables: https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions/1784178
questions.audience: General public, Scottish and northern residents
questions.verdict: Because Scotland often produces more wind power than the grid can carry south. Putting demand next to it reduces the waste.
questions.answer: Scotland's wind farms sometimes generate more than the grid can move to where people use it. When that happens they are paid to switch off, which adds 'constraint costs' to the system. A Royal Academy of Engineering presentation to the government's AI Energy Council put UK wind curtailment at 8.3 TWh in 2024. Data centres placed near that surplus could use power that would otherwise be thrown away. That is why the AI Growth Zone discounts are largest in Scotland. Today almost all of Britain's capacity runs the other way: about two-thirds of colocation IT load is in London, which is already among the most congested parts of the grid.

figures.quote: UK wind curtailment of 8.3 TWh in 2024 represents a significant untapped opportunity.
figures.publisher: AI Energy Council minutes (Royal Academy of Engineering presentation)
figures.check_note: Quote found in the minutes. 8.3 TWh in 2024 matches.

figures.claim: Constraint-cost rationale
figures.quote: For example, at times, the amount of wind generation in Scotland may be more than the grid is currently capable of handling – resulting in so called “constraint costs”.
figures.check_note: Quote found on Delivering AI Growth Zones.

figures.claim: Largest AIGZ discount is in Scotland
figures.quote: For a 500 MW data centre this will be up to: £24/MWh in Scotland £16/MWh in Cumbria £14/MWh in the North East
figures.check_note: Quote found ('For a 500 MW data centre this will be up to...'). £14 to £24 per MWh matches.

figures.quote: London 1,048
figures.check_note: 'London 1,048' is in the table. The rows add up to 1,566 MW, and 1048/1566 = 66.9%, about 67. The share is Hum's calculation.

The page did not say whether London is 'among the most congested parts of the grid'; that is general context, not a sourced figure. Hum should source it or drop the phrase.

questions.q: Will new UK data centres run England short of water?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A run of 2026 written questions: Q27760 on AI data centres and 'long-term national water demand forecasts', Q28747 on demand 'in each water-resource zone', HL3327 on requiring operators to report water use, and Essex and East of England constituency questions: https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions/1940097 ; https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions/1926511
questions.audience: Residents in water-stressed areas (East and South East England), students
questions.verdict: Nobody knows yet. There is no national figure, and some water companies have already said no to data centres.
questions.answer: The UK has no published figure for how much water its data centres use or will use. Defra says it is still building the evidence, and there is no rule requiring operators to report. The Environment Agency's 2025 national water framework warns that data centres could be a large new demand. It notes that some water companies have already refused applications for water from data centres, and that many could be built before big new reservoirs and transfers arrive. AI Growth Zone applicants must state their expected water needs and show that the local supplier can provide them. How much water a site uses depends heavily on its cooling design: closed-loop systems use far less than evaporative cooling.

figures.quote: Some water companies have already refused applications for water from data centres.
figures.publisher: Environment Agency, National Framework for Water Resources 2025
figures.check_note: Quote found in chapter 9 of the National Framework for Water Resources 2025.

figures.claim: Timing risk relative to new water infrastructure
figures.quote: It is also likely to result in a large and rapid increase in the number of data centres in England, with many being built by 2030 and before the large strategic water resource options have come online.
figures.publisher: Environment Agency, National Framework for Water Resources 2025
figures.check_note: Quote found on the same water framework page.

figures.claim: No government estimate of data-centre water demand yet
figures.quote: Defra is working with the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, the Environment Agency and water companies to improve understanding of data centre water demand.
figures.check_note: Quote matches WQ 1926511.

figures.claim: AI Growth Zone water requirement
figures.quote: AI Growth Zone applicants are also required to provide details of their anticipated water requirements and evidence from the relevant water supplier on the availability of supply.
figures.check_note: Quote matches WQ 1940097.

gaps: No measured UK data-centre water consumption exists; MOSL's planned data-centre water dashboard has not been found published.

DSIT's Compute Evidence Annex says UK AI water use in 2035 'could range between 0.1–0.5 trillion cubic metres'. That conflicts with its own Figure 9 axis (millions m3) and is implausibly large compared with total national water use. Do not use it until DSIT clarifies.
No per-site water figures for the named AI Growth Zones.

questions.q: How much will AI add to the UK's carbon emissions?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Q101285 asked for an assessment of AI data-centre demand on net zero targets. Q2680 asked how the government will 'balance its updated emissions estimates of data centres' with the fifth carbon budget. Q108617 asked whether the Climate Change Committee's Seventh Carbon Budget includes data-centre energy: https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions?searchTerm=%22data%20centres%22&take=100&tabledWhenFrom=2025-01-01
questions.verdict: The government's model gives 34 to 123 million tonnes of CO2 over 2025 to 2035, about 1 to 3% of UK emissions.
questions.answer: DSIT's 2026 model, corrected in April, estimates that UK AI computing could cause 34 to 123 million tonnes of CO2 in total between 2025 and 2035. That is roughly 0.9 to 3.4% of all projected UK emissions over the decade. These are scenario estimates, not measurements. Most of the emissions come from the power stations supplying data centres and from building them. Which end of the range happens depends mainly on how fast the grid decarbonises. In 2025, fossil fuels, mostly gas, still made 36% of UK electricity (Ember). If the government's Clean Power 2030 goal is met, the result would be near the bottom of the range.

figures.claim: Cumulative UK GHG emissions from AI compute 2025-2035 (DSIT model)
figures.quote: we estimate that UK greenhouse gas emissions from AI compute over the 10 years from 2025 to 2035 could range from 34 to 123 MtCO₂ (Figure 7).
figures.check_note: Quote found in the annex PDF, and confirmed as the corrected text on the corrections page (changes of 20 April 2026). 34 to 123 MtCO2 matches.

figures.claim: Share of UK projected total emissions over 2025-2035
figures.quote: This is around 0.9-3.4% of the UK’s projected total emissions over the 10 year period.
figures.check_note: Quote found on the corrections page. 0.9 to 3.4% matches.

figures.claim: Fossil share of UK electricity 2025
figures.quote: relied on fossil fuels for 36% of its electricity in 2025
figures.check_note: Quote found on the Ember United Kingdom page. 36% fossil in 2025 matches.

figures.claim: Clean Power 2030 target referenced
figures.unit: % of GB generation from clean sources by 2030
figures.quote: The current government plan is that by 2030, the UK power system will see clean sources produce at least 95% of Great Britain’s generation
figures.check_note: Quote found in the annex PDF. 'At least 95%' of GB generation from clean sources by 2030 matches.

gaps: The DSIT model rests on McKinsey compute-demand projections that are not published in full; the annual TWh behind Figure 10 is not given as numbers in the text.
UK grid carbon intensity in g/kWh for 2025 was not found on the Ember page as text.
Whether the CCC's Seventh Carbon Budget explicitly models data centres was not checked.

questions.q: Is streaming TV worse for the UK grid than normal broadcast TV, and is using AI at work better or worse than doing it by hand?
questions.evidence_people_ask: DESNZ commissioned two Europe Economics studies (2025, follow-up 2026) to answer exactly this public question about digital services versus physical alternatives. Parliamentary interest in data-centre demand from everyday digital services shows up across the PQs listed at https://questions-statements-api.parliament.uk/api/writtenquestions/questions/1922602
questions.verdict: In the government study, streaming used more electricity than broadcast TV. AI-assisted office tasks used less than doing them by hand.
questions.answer: A 2026 study for DESNZ by Europe Economics compared digital services with their old-fashioned equivalents. If every UK viewer of broadcast TV (Freeview-style) switched to streaming, electricity demand would rise by about 1.8 TWh a year. That is around 0.6% of UK demand and is mostly driven by the cost of moving the data. For AI-assisted office tasks such as drafting emails or transcription, the digital option used less electricity than doing the work manually in every scenario. That is because workers finish faster, so less office power is used per task. These are modelled, stylised estimates: they assume no change in how much people watch or work.

figures.claim: Net UK electricity increase if all broadcast TV (DTT) viewing moved to streaming
figures.quote: We conducted further analysis on the potential UK electricity impact of shifting all current users of broadcast television (DTT) to video streaming, and found that this could increase UK electricity demand by around 1.8 TWh.
figures.check_note: Quote found in the follow-up report PDF. About 1.8 TWh matches.

figures.claim: That increase as a share of UK demand
figures.quote: around 0.6 per cent of total UK electricity demand, which was 319 TWh in 2024.
figures.check_note: Quote found. 'Around 0.6 per cent' matches; 1.8/319 = 0.56%.

figures.claim: AI-assisted office tasks vs manual
figures.quote: For all AI-assisted office tasks, the digital option consistently consumes less electricity than the manual alternative across low, medium and high scenarios.
figures.check_note: Quote found in the follow-up report PDF.

gaps: The per-task kWh values in the study's Table 1.1 have an unclear functional unit on the page, so they are not quoted as per-hour or per-task figures.
The study deliberately ignores rebound effects (more use because it is cheaper or easier), so it cannot say whether AI raises or lowers total UK demand.

questions.q: How much electricity do data centres in Africa use compared with the US?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Not verified on a forum: my web-search budget ran out before I could find threads. The IEA's Energy and AI report answers this region-by-region question directly, which suggests demand for it, but that is not proof of reader questions. https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai/energy-demand-from-ai
questions.verdict: Very little: under 1 kWh per person a year in Africa, against about 540 kWh per person in the US.
questions.answer: The IEA estimates that in 2024 data centres used less than 1 kWh of electricity per person in Africa. That is the lowest of any region. In the United States the figure was about 540 kWh per person, so more than 500 times higher. These are consumption figures, meaning electricity used, not generated. The IEA forecasts that Africa will rise to slightly less than 2 kWh per person by 2030. South Africa grows fastest, to more than 25 kWh per person. US use per person is forecast to pass 1,200 kWh. All the future numbers are IEA projections, not measurements.

questions.q: Should Africa build AI data centres when 600 million people there still have no electricity?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Not verified on a forum (search budget exhausted). The tension is a common framing in coverage of the Microsoft/G42 Kenya project: https://news.microsoft.com/source/2024/05/22/microsoft-and-g42-announce-1-billion-comprehensive-digital-ecosystem-initiative-for-kenya/
questions.verdict: For now, data centres are a tiny share of Africa's electricity. The bigger gap is the roughly 600 million people in sub-Saharan Africa without any power.
questions.answer: About 600 million people in sub-Saharan Africa had no electricity in 2023, according to the IEA. That is most of the world's 750 million without it. Data centres in Africa currently use less than 1 kWh per person a year, so today they compete very little with homes for power. A single large facility, though, can still strain a weak local grid. The IEA expects that across emerging and developing economies, data centres will make up only around 5% of electricity demand growth to 2030. Whether new data centres speed up or slow down access depends on who pays for new power plants and grids. Hum has no source that settles that question.

questions.q: Why do people living near data centres complain about a constant hum?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Residents of Great Oak (Prince William County, VA) protested in August 2022 carrying signs about noise from four Amazon data centres (Prince William Times, https://www.princewilliamtimes.com/news/some-cities-suffering-from-data-center-noise-turn-to-tough-limits/article_2aa7fb8c-b6aa-11ed-8626-5738aae2f76c.html). Web search budget was exhausted, so no Reddit/PAA evidence was gathered.
questions.audience: Residents near existing or proposed data centres
questions.verdict: The noise comes mostly from cooling fans and chillers, and it bothers people because it never stops, more than because it is loud.
questions.answer: Data centres run cooling equipment day and night. In Chandler, Arizona, residents traced a high-pitched hum to a data centre's air-conditioning units. Near a cluster of Amazon data centres in Prince William County, Virginia, measurements found the noise was below the county's 60-decibel daytime limit about half the time. Residents still said the drone, especially at night, cost them sleep. The local paper put it this way: the problem is less the loudness than the constancy. Amazon said it would muffle its cooling equipment and replace its rooftop fans. These are documented local cases, not a measured national picture.

questions.q: How loud is a data centre allowed to be near homes?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Local rezoning fights where developers proposed data centres within 600 feet of housing and the county debated noise limits (Prince William Times, https://www.princewilliamtimes.com/news/some-cities-suffering-from-data-center-noise-turn-to-tough-limits/article_2aa7fb8c-b6aa-11ed-8626-5738aae2f76c.html). Fairfax County wrote noise-study rules into its 2024 data-centre zoning amendment (https://www.fairfaxcounty.gov/planning-development/data-centers).
questions.verdict: It depends on local law. One Virginia county allows 60 dB by day and 55 dB at night in residential areas, while normal background near data centres is about 45 to 50 dB.
questions.answer: No single national limit exists. It is set by local noise ordinances. In 2023, Prince William County, Virginia, allowed 60 decibels by day and 55 at night in residential areas, and it exempted air-conditioning noise. An acoustics expert quoted by the local paper said background noise near data centres is typically 45 to 50 decibels. Since 2024, Fairfax County has required a noise study before a data centre is approved, with all cooling equipment modelled at full load, and a second study with field measurements after it is built. Decibels are logarithmic, so a source 10 dB above background sounds roughly twice as loud.

questions.q: How often do data centre backup diesel generators actually run?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Virginia lawmakers debated generator emissions 'even just during the testing hours each month' (Virginia Mercury via Royal Examiner, https://royalexaminer.com/lawmakers-debate-how-to-regulate-data-centers-diesel-backup-generators). questions.verdict: Rarely for real outages, but they are started for testing regularly, and US rules allow up to 100 hours a year of non-emergency running.
questions.answer: Most of the time, they sit idle. A Microsoft engineer said in 2020 that the company starts its generators once a month, load-tests them once a year, and that they cover an outage less than once a year on average (a company statement). US federal rules for emergency engines put no limit on running in a real emergency. They allow up to 100 hours a year for maintenance and readiness, and up to 50 of those hours in other non-emergency situations. In Fairfax County, Virginia, testing is exempt from the noise rules only between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m., for no more than two hours a day.

questions.q: Is the exhaust from data centre diesel generators bad for your health?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Virginia Delegate Guzman told a 2026 committee that generator pollutants are linked to asthma ER visits (Virginia Mercury via Royal Examiner, https://royalexaminer.com/lawmakers-debate-how-to-regulate-data-centers-diesel-backup-generators). questions.verdict: Diesel exhaust is a known human carcinogen. How much harm comes from one site depends on how many hours it runs and how close you live, and no one has measured that for most sites.

A Virginia lawmaker told a 2026 committee that pollutants from standby generators are linked to heart and lung disease and to emergency-room visits for asthma. What is not known for most sites is the actual exposure next door, because generators run few hours and local monitoring is rare. Virginia lawmakers have proposed a one-year state study of what permitted standby generators emit.

questions.q: How much harm does air pollution from data centres do to public health?
questions.evidence_people_ask: UC Riverside/Caltech 'Unpaid Toll' study widely covered (UCR News, https://news.ucr.edu/articles/2024/12/09/ais-deadly-air-pollution-toll); Virginia lawmakers cited new research on generator pollution in 2026 (https://royalexaminer.com/lawmakers-debate-how-to-regulate-data-centers-diesel-backup-generators).
questions.verdict: One study estimates up to about 1,300 early deaths a year in the US by 2030, mostly from power-plant pollution. It is a model forecast, not a count.
questions.answer: Researchers at UC Riverside and Caltech modelled the air pollution from US data centres, both from the power plants that generate their electricity and from backup diesel generators. They project 940 to 1,590 early deaths a year by 2030, about 1,300 in the middle, and health costs approaching $20 billion a year. For Northern Virginia's generators alone, they estimated $190 to $260 million a year in regional health costs, rising tenfold if the generators emitted their full permitted amounts. These are model estimates from EPA health-risk tools, not observed deaths. The arXiv preprint's later version gives 2028 figures, so its numbers may have changed.

questions.q: Can data centres run their diesel generators to help the grid during heatwaves or cold snaps?
questions.evidence_people_ask: In January 2026 the US Department of Energy let PJM data centres run on generators during a cold snap, which Virginia lawmakers then debated (Virginia Mercury via Royal Examiner, https://royalexaminer.com/lawmakers-debate-how-to-regulate-data-centers-diesel-backup-generators).
questions.verdict: Normally only a little, but in a declared emergency the US government has let them go over their permits.
questions.answer: US federal rules allow emergency generators up to 50 hours a year of non-emergency running, which counts toward a 100-hour yearly cap on maintenance and readiness use. In a real emergency there is no time limit. During the cold snap at the end of January 2026, the US Department of Energy allowed data centres on the PJM grid to run fully on generators, even above their permitted emissions. PJM said no data centres in Dominion Energy's zone, which covers much of Virginia, actually needed to switch over. Switching takes the load off the grid, but it moves the pollution to the neighbourhood.

questions.q: How close to my house can a data centre be built?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A developer proposed up to 14 data centres within 600 feet of housing in Prince William County (Prince William Times, https://www.princewilliamtimes.com/news/some-cities-suffering-from-data-center-noise-turn-to-tough-limits/article_2aa7fb8c-b6aa-11ed-8626-5738aae2f76c.html). Fairfax County adopted data-centre distance rules in September 2024 (https://www.fairfaxcounty.gov/planning-development/data-centers).
questions.verdict: It is set locally. Fairfax County, Virginia, requires at least 200 feet from homes, and many places have no specific rule.
questions.answer: No national rule exists in the US. It is up to local zoning. Fairfax County, Virginia, adopted rules in September 2024: a data-centre building must sit at least 200 feet from a residential lot line, and ground-level equipment such as generators and cooling units must be 300 feet away or screened from homes by the building itself. Exceptions are possible by special approval. In neighbouring Prince William County, one developer proposed up to 14 data centres within 600 feet of housing. As the local paper noted, noise fades with distance, so the gap from your home is one of the main protections.

questions.q: Are there cleaner alternatives to diesel backup generators at data centres?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Virginia's 2026 HB 507 originally required battery storage as the main backup and was amended to require Tier IV generators (Virginia Mercury via Royal Examiner, https://royalexaminer.com/lawmakers-debate-how-to-regulate-data-centers-diesel-backup-generators).
questions.verdict: Cleaner diesel engines, batteries and hydrogen fuel cells all exist, but only the cleaner engines are widespread, and company goals are not yet proven.
questions.answer: There are three main options. The first is cleaner diesel: a 2026 Virginia bill would stop air permits for data centres whose generators fall below Tier IV, the cleanest emissions tier, for applications after July 2026. The second is batteries: that bill originally made batteries the main backup, but the requirement was cut. The third is hydrogen: in 2020 Microsoft said a 250-kilowatt fuel cell had powered a row of servers for 48 hours, and it aimed to end its reliance on diesel by 2030. Microsoft says diesel is under 1% of its emissions. These are company claims, and progress toward the 2030 goal has not been checked.

questions.verdict: A lot, and the number is rising fast: tens of billions of dollars of projects every quarter in 2026, by one tracker's count.
questions.answer: Data Center Watch counted $18 billion of US projects blocked and $46 billion delayed between 2023 and March 2025. By the end of 2025 its total had reached about $152 billion. A delay is not a cancellation, and the dollar values are investment, not electricity. The tracker publishes no detailed method.

questions.q: Do data centres pay their way in local taxes, or get tax breaks?
questions.evidence_people_ask: State legislators commissioned audits (Virginia's JLARC), and Good Jobs First's report on state budget losses was widely covered: https://goodjobsfirst.org/cloudy-with-a-loss-of-spending-control-how-data-centers-are-endangering-state-budgets/. Data Center Watch also tracks a Virginia effort to repeal the tax break: https://www.datacenterwatch.org/
questions.verdict: Both. They can pay large local property taxes while getting large state sales-tax exemptions.
questions.answer: In Virginia, Loudoun County officials expected data-centre tax revenue to approach $900 million in fiscal 2025, close to the county's whole operating budget. Virginia's state sales-tax exemption for data-centre equipment cost $732 million in 2024, according to Good Jobs First's reading of the state's audited report. Across the US, 32 states offer tax incentives to data centres, and 12 of them do not disclose what the incentives cost. In Texas, the projected cost for fiscal 2025 went from $130 million to $1 billion in 23 months. So whether a data centre 'pays its way' depends on whether you count local or state taxes.

questions.q: How much money do states give up in data centre tax breaks?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Washington State set up a task force that will examine 'the jobs created' by data centres against their tax breaks (reported by Good Jobs First): https://goodjobsfirst.org/cloudy-with-a-loss-of-spending-control-how-data-centers-are-endangering-state-budgets/ . questions.audience: Taxpayers, state legislators, students writing on public finance
questions.verdict: Billions a year, and the cost is rising fast. In four states it is now over $1 billion a year each.
questions.answer: Most of the cost comes from exemptions on the sales tax data centres would otherwise pay on servers and equipment. The watchdog Good Jobs First (June 2026) counts 37 states with these exemptions. It says the cost already exceeds $1 billion a year in at least four of them. These are official cost estimates of tax not collected, not money paid out. Fourteen states publish no cost figure at all, so the national total is unknown.

questions.q: Do states earn back the tax they give up on data centres?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Virginia commissioned a legislative audit (JLARC 2024) to answer this. Good Jobs First's 2026 disclosure report pulls together the three state return-on-investment studies: https://goodjobsfirst.org/data-center-tax-abatements-why-states-and-localities-must-disclose-these-soaring-revenue-losses/
questions.verdict: Not at state level. The three states that measured it got back less than they gave up, though local governments can come out ahead.
questions.answer: Three US states have measured the return on their data-centre tax exemptions. Each found that the extra economic activity brought back less state tax than the exemption cost, losing 52 to 91 cents of every dollar given up. In Virginia, the state loses about 52 cents per dollar. Local governments are a different case. They often gain from property and equipment taxes (see the Loudoun question), so 'winners and losers' depends on which government you look at. Virginia's exemption took 81.3% of the state's whole economic-development incentive budget in FY2024.

questions.q: Do data centres lower local property taxes for residents?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Loudoun County, Virginia, runs a dedicated public page that answers residents' questions on data-centre tax revenue and the county budget: https://www.loudoun.gov/6409/Data-Centers-Tax-Revenues-County-Budget
questions.verdict: In Loudoun County, Virginia, yes: equipment taxes on data centres have helped cut homeowners' rate. The county warns this growth will level off.
questions.answer: Local governments tax the expensive servers inside data centres as business personal property. In Loudoun, the world's biggest data-centre cluster, that rate is $4.15 per $100 of assessed value. The county says this revenue helped it cut homeowners' real property tax rate from $1.145 per $100 in 2016 to $0.805 in 2026, about 30% lower. It also funded schools, police and parks. The county itself warns that data-centre equipment revenue 'will plateau in the next five to 10 years', after which rates may need to rise. This is one county's experience. Places that grant property-tax abatements get far less.

questions.q: Are ordinary households paying for data centres' power through their electricity bills?
questions.evidence_people_ask: A Harvard Electricity Law Initiative paper (March 2025) on this exact question was widely covered: https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/extracting-profits-from-the-public-how-utility-ratepayers-are-paying-for-big-techs-power/
questions.verdict: Possibly, through how grid costs are shared, but there is no single sourced dollar figure yet.
questions.answer: Utilities build new power lines and plants for big data centres, and the cost is normally shared among all customers. Harvard researchers Ari Peskoe and Eliza Martin argue that discounted special contracts mean 'ratepayers share the costs of that expansion'. They also note many of these contracts are secret, which makes the shift hard to measure. Their paper is a legal and policy analysis, and it gives no dollar figure per household. Regulators in several states are now writing special tariffs for large users to limit this. Hum has not yet sourced a measured bill impact.

questions.q: How many data centres are there in the world?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Statista runs a page titled 'Number of data centers worldwide 2026, by country or territory', updated Sep 2026, which shows the question gets asked often (https://www.statista.com/statistics/1228433/data-centers-worldwide-by-country/). Epoch AI's data hub has an FAQ built around questions like 'What are the largest AI data centers?' (https://epoch.ai/data/ai-data-centers). This turn's web-search budget was used up, so I could not collect Reddit or People-also-ask evidence.
questions.verdict: No one keeps an official global count. Directories list thousands of data centres, and their numbers disagree.
questions.answer: No official census of data centres exists. Commercial directories count facilities in different ways. Statista reported 4,767 in the US in April 2026, while Cloudscene's live directory lists 5,427 US facilities. Directories also undercount some countries: Cloudscene lists only 449 in China. The best-tracked group is the largest sites. Synergy Research counted 1,360 hyperscale data centres at the end of 2025, holding 48% of the world's data-centre capacity (analyst estimates). Counting buildings also misleads, because sizes run from server rooms to sites drawing over 1,000 MW. That is why Hum, like the IEA, measures electricity consumption (485 TWh in 2025) instead of buildings.

questions.q: What is a 'hyperscale' data centre, and how many are there?
questions.evidence_people_ask: The term turns up in almost every news story about AI data centres, and the IEA's 2026 report has to define it ('the largest data centre operators – so-called hyperscalers'), which suggests readers need it explained (https://www.iea.org/reports/powering-artificial-intelligence/executive-summary). questions.verdict: Hyperscale means the giant data centres run by the biggest cloud and internet companies. There are about 1,360, and they hold nearly half the world's capacity.
questions.answer: 'Hyperscale' refers to the large data centres run by the biggest cloud and internet firms, such as Amazon, Microsoft and Google. Synergy Research counted 1,360 at the end of 2025, up from 1,136 a year earlier, and says they hold 48% of the world's data-centre capacity. Amazon, Microsoft and Google alone held 59% of hyperscale capacity in early 2025. Synergy forecasts that hyperscalers will hold 67% of all capacity by 2031. These are analyst counts, not official statistics. The IEA says hyperscalers will spend more than USD 700 billion on capital projects in 2026, mostly new data centres.

questions.q: What is the biggest AI data centre in the world right now?
questions.evidence_people_ask: Epoch AI's data hub answers 'What are the largest AI data centers?' as a headline FAQ (https://epoch.ai/data/ai-data-centers), and Epoch publishes a recurring 'record for computing capacity in a single data center' tracker (https://epoch.ai/data-insights/largest-data-center-compute). Search evidence was not collected because the budget was exhausted.
questions.verdict: By Epoch AI's satellite-based estimate it is Colossus 2 in Memphis, drawing about 946 MW of IT power. That title changes every few months.
questions.answer: Epoch AI builds independent estimates from satellite images, permits and filings. On those estimates, the largest operating AI data centre is Colossus 2 in Memphis (owned by SpaceXAI, formerly xAI), drawing about 946 MW of IT power. Next come Anthropic-Amazon New Carlisle in Indiana (910 MW) and Microsoft Fairwater Atlanta (636 MW). Epoch projects Colossus 2 will reach 1,531 MW in early 2027. These are estimates, not company figures, and IT power leaves out cooling: Epoch says total facility power is 20–50% higher. The record keeps falling. The largest single site's computing capacity has doubled every seven months since August 2024.

questions.q: How many homes could a 1-gigawatt data centre power?
questions.evidence_people_ask: News stories routinely translate data-centre gigawatts into homes. CNBC quoted OpenAI's CFO doing exactly this for Abilene (https://www.cnbc.com/2025/09/23/openai-first-data-center-in-500-billion-stargate-project-up-in-texas.html), and the EIA keeps an FAQ 'How much electricity does an American home use?' (https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=97&t=3). Search evidence was not collected because the budget was exhausted.
questions.verdict: Roughly 500,000 to 800,000 average US homes' worth of electricity, depending on how hard the site runs.
questions.answer: A gigawatt is a rate of power, not an amount of energy. Running flat out for a year, 1 GW uses 8.76 TWh. The average US home bought 10,791 kWh in 2022 (EIA), so that is about 812,000 homes' worth (our calculation). Epoch AI says AI data centres typically average 60–80% of capacity, which gives roughly 490,000–650,000 homes. OpenAI's finance chief told CNBC that a gigawatt is about 750,000 US homes. The IEA says a typical AI-focused data centre already uses as much as 100,000 households, and the largest under construction will use 20 times as much. Homes in other countries use less, so they would count higher.

figures.check_note: Verbatim: 'In 2022, the average annual amount of electricity sold to (purchased by) a U.S. residential electric-utility customer was 10,791 kilowatthours (kWh), an average of about 899 kWh per month.' Matches.

figures.quote: However, the average power consumption of these data centers is typically 60–80% of capacity, due to idle time and maintenance.
figures.check_note: Quote verbatim (60–80% of capacity, due to idle time and maintenance). The home counts are derived: 8.76e9/10,791 = 811,788 (about 812,000) and x0.6 = 487,073 (about 487,000). Low/mid are consistent; the 80% end (about 649,000) is left out of high (null).

figures.check_note: Fetched with curl after WebFetch got a 403. Verbatim: 'The campus has the potential to ultimately scale past a gigawatt of capacity, OpenAI finance chief Sarah Friar told CNBC. That would be enough electricity to power about 750,000 U.S. homes.'
